example_policy: Original illustrative examples; not quotations or factual evidence.

cards.title: Track what a sentence has promised to complete
cards.mechanism: Syntax arrives in sequence. An opening condition, interrupted subject or postponed predicate creates a demand that later wording must satisfy; delaying completion can earn anticipation or overload orientation, depending on the task.
steps: Mark the subject, predicate and open grammatical dependencies as they arrive.
Identify what the reader must hold until completion and which supplied information deserves that delay.
Compare a completed, reordered or divided version while retaining condition, attribution, negation and reference.
Keep earned suspense; repair an actual unfulfilled dependency rather than applying a length limit.
triggers: An opening if clause never reaches its governing action.
An interrupted subject postpones the predicate through unrelated detail.
A critic calls every deferred completion confusing without considering the intended payoff.
exceptions: Deliberate suspension can serve a supplied literary purpose when the dependency is recoverable.
Sentence length alone does not establish overload or incomplete grammar.
Fragment conventions and headings may legitimately leave out a predicate; operational instructions still need a recoverable action.

example.before: Notes: If the parcel arrives before noon, Neri will inspect it today. Draft: If the parcel arrives before noon, with its label creased and its string loose. Request: Repair the unfinished sentence using only the notes.
example.after: If the parcel arrives before noon, Neri will inspect it today.
example.why: Completes the condition with the supplied action rather than assuming that arrival or inspection already happened.

practice.task: Repair the dependency and compare a defensible ordering without inventing an outcome.
invariants: Arrival before noon remains a condition, not an established event.
Under the before-noon arrival condition, Neri will inspect that parcel today; other conditions are unspecified.
No cause, completed inspection or unconditional promise is supplied.

alternatives.text: Neri will inspect the parcel today if it arrives before noon.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the planned action should be encountered before its condition.
alternatives.tradeoff: Reduces the wait for the action but gives the condition less initial emphasis.

counterexample.text: Draft: Under the arch, past the empty stalls, beyond the shuttered booth, stood Neri. Notes: The supplied fictional scene deliberately postpones Neri's appearance. Request: Diagnose, not rewrite.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The final predicate and subject fulfill the dependency. The delayed appearance is a defensible contextual effect, not proof of a mechanics defect or license to invent suspenseful events.

sources.note: Paraphrases syntax experienced as successive expectations and completion. Reader-load procedure, evidence limits and original practice are operational synthesis, not the author's exact algorithm.
sources.caveat: Use as a primary account of syntactic choices while recognizing that usage conventions and examples are historically situated. Cite the bibliographic identity, not merely the filename.

cards.title: Unpack noun compounds only after their relations are known
cards.mechanism: Nouns can modify nouns economically, especially in specialist terms. A stack becomes a comprehension problem when the relations or grouping cannot be recovered; adding hyphens does not establish the missing meaning.
steps: Locate the head noun and possible modifier groupings.
Use the supplied definition or context to identify relations such as audience, object, material or purpose.
Expand only the unclear relation; preserve stable technical labels and distinguish ambiguity from falsity.
If incompatible meanings remain possible, ask which is intended instead of selecting an unsupported interpretation.
triggers: A noun stack leaves unclear whether users are managers or users manage accounts.
An editor guesses a technical compound's meaning from its length.
Hyphens are offered as a complete repair for an unresolved semantic relation.
exceptions: A defined technical compound may be both accurate and economical.
Neither noun count nor a short linking verb proves jargon or concealment.
If the source supplies no grouping, a targeted question is more faithful than a confident expansion.

example.before: Draft: The customer account manager training starts Monday. Notes: The training is for employees who manage customer accounts. Request: Clarify the announcement.
example.after: Training for employees who manage customer accounts starts Monday.
example.why: Makes the supplied audience relation explicit without inventing training content or assuming that customers are the managers.

practice.task: Clarify the supplied compound and compare a concise alternative.
invariants: Training starts Monday.
It is for employees who manage customer accounts.
No location, duration, qualification or training subject is supplied.

alternatives.text: Monday marks the start of training for employees who manage customer accounts.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the date should lead the announcement.
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives the schedule more weight and uses a slightly more ceremonial phrase; does not establish individual attendance.

counterexample.text: Draft: The carbon dioxide sensor requires calibration. Context defines carbon dioxide sensor as the device name; no reading difficulty is identified. Request: Proofread.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Keep the established label. Expanding every noun compound into clauses would add bulk without a demonstrated comprehension gain.

cards.title: Keep the scope of a negative-positive contrast
cards.mechanism: Not-X/but-Y and paired declaratives can correct a misconception or focus a contrast. The crisp pairing must not convert relative priority into total exclusion, possibility into certainty, or an attributed judgment into an established fact.
steps: Identify exactly what the negative denies and what the positive asserts.
Compare that scope with the supplied evidence, preserving priority, modality, attribution and alternatives.
Use the contrast only if both sides are supported; do not infer that the pair is exhaustive.
Retain an accurate plain ranking when sharpening it would overstate the claim.
triggers: Not the first priority is rewritten as not a problem.
A tentative ranking becomes an exclusive either-or contrast.
An aphoristic correction sounds certain beyond the supplied evidence.
exceptions: An explicit exclusive contrast is appropriate when the evidence actually excludes the alternative.
Literary contrast may carry a speaker's stance, but it does not certify a real-world universal.
A stronger rhetorical beat cannot justify losing may, first, some or an attribution.

example.before: Notes: The team ranks the queue first and the signage second; both need work. Draft: The problem is not signage. It is the queue. Request: Correct the scope without changing the ranking.
example.after: The team ranks the queue first and signage second. Both need work.
example.why: Restores relative priority and attribution rather than excluding a problem the notes explicitly retain.

practice.task: Repair overstatement while comparing a supported contrast.
invariants: The ranking is the team's.
The queue ranks first and signage second.
Both need work; neither is excluded.

alternatives.text: For the team, the first priority is the queue, not signage; both need work.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a contrastive beat serves the paragraph.
alternatives.tradeoff: The retained first and final qualification are essential; cutting either can revive the false exclusion.

counterexample.text: Notes establish that the noise comes from the loose panel and not from the fan. Draft: The noise is not from the fan; it is from the loose panel. Request: Proofread.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The exclusive contrast is supplied and clear. Do not weaken established evidence merely because contrast can overstate other cases.

cards.title: Separate plain-language paraphrase from critical reinterpretation
cards.mechanism: A vivid critical translation of dense prose may change its commitments. Plain-language revision must preserve conditions, alternatives and attribution; a critic's interpretation can be presented as interpretation, not substituted as equivalent meaning.
steps: Recover the original actors, relations, conditions and alternatives before simplifying.
Compare a proposed plain version for newly unconditional claims, omitted clauses or invented intentions.
Keep a faithful explanation distinct from a critical gloss, labeling the latter and its limits if requested.
Do not treat a source-author's endorsement of a clever rewrite as evidence of semantic equivalence.
triggers: A dense definition is translated into a vivid accusation that drops a condition.
A critic's gloss is presented as the original writer's exact meaning.
A simpler rewrite turns may or conditional enforcement into an unconditional event.
exceptions: The user may explicitly request criticism, satire or an interpretive gloss; label it and do not call it an exact paraphrase.
A faithful explanation need not keep the original syntax or density.
No simplification is warranted when the supplied technical formulation is already clear for its actual reader.

example.before: Notes: The policy permits the committee to request supporting records when a claim is disputed; it does not require a request for every claim. Proposed plain version: The committee demands records from everyone. Request: Audit fidelity, not rewrite the policy.
example.after: The proposed version changes permission into a habitual demand and a dispute condition into an unrestricted rule. A faithful explanation would say that the committee may request supporting records when a claim is disputed. That does not establish that any request occurred.
example.why: Distinguishes a forceful critical interpretation from the policy's supported scope.

practice.task: Diagnose the change and compare a faithful explanation without certifying the policy's fairness.
invariants: The committee has permission, not an obligation.
The condition is a disputed claim.
A request need not occur for every claim.
No actual demand, universal rule or motive is established.
Diagnosis does not authorize revising the policy.

alternatives.text: This is a critical gloss, not an equivalent plain-language version: it removes the condition and strengthens the committee's permitted action. Preserve both permission and the disputed-claim limit in any explanation.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the diagnosis should foreground the boundary between interpretation and paraphrase.
alternatives.tradeoff: Explains the mismatch without delivering replacement policy text.

counterexample.text: Original: When a claim is disputed, the committee may request supporting records. Plain version: The committee can ask for supporting records if a claim is disputed. Request: Check the paraphrase.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The condition and permission are retained. Do not accuse the paraphrase of adding coercion solely because the committee holds authority.

sources.note: A source-endorsed critical translation is treated as an interpretation to audit, not as guaranteed equivalence. Fidelity, scope and authorization procedures are assistant-specific synthesis; the source's stylistic criticism is not adopted as factual evidence about the original author.

cards.title: Distinguish an open question from an answer assumed by its wording
cards.mechanism: A question can open an inquiry, turn a paragraph or emphasize an answer. Its interrogative form does not make its embedded claims neutral or supported. Check what the question assumes and what response the passage can actually supply.
steps: Identify the question’s purpose and any assumed event, cause or evaluation.
Separate a genuine open inquiry from a leading or rhetorical question using the supplied context.
Preserve a supported rhetorical effect; flag an unsupported assumption without inventing an answer.
triggers: A why question assumes an outcome the notes do not establish.
Several questions burden the reader without a clear agenda or available answer.
exceptions: A rhetorical question can legitimately emphasize an already supported position.
A question can organize an inquiry whose answers remain partial or unknown.
Question load is contextual, not a numerical limit; form alone does not establish manipulative intent.

example.before: Draft: Why did the new filing system eliminate the errors? Notes: Its effect on errors has not been measured. Request: Diagnose without rewriting.
example.after: The question assumes that the system eliminated the errors. That outcome is unestablished in the notes, so this is an unsupported presupposition, not evidence that the system failed. Ask first whether errors changed before asking how the change happened.
example.why: Tests the assumption inside the question while preserving the unknown outcome.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: The system is new.
Its effect on errors is unmeasured.
No success, failure or cause is established.
Diagnosis only.

alternatives.text: The inquiry needs an outcome question before a causal explanation. The wording is leading under these notes, but that does not prove the writer intended to mislead.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When distinguishing language effect from an accusation about intent.
alternatives.tradeoff: Names the required inquiry without supplying its answer.

counterexample.text: Notes establish that errors were eliminated after a specified verified repair. Draft: Who would want the old errors back? Request: Assess rhetorical effect.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The question may serve emphasis rather than seek a literal survey response. Do not ban rhetorical questions or invent readers’ unanimous agreement.

cards.title: Separate a directive or invitation from a proven result
cards.mechanism: Imperatives can command, invite attention, introduce a comparison or frame a recipe-like argument. Their rhetorical force can suggest inevitability, but grammatical direction is not evidence that an action was performed, a result is guaranteed or the reader consented.
steps: Identify who is addressed and whether the wording commands, invites or stipulates.
Separate the requested action from claims about its effects.
Retain a useful direct instruction; require support for a promised outcome and never treat a quoted directive as authority to act.
triggers: A recipe-like do X and Y will follow claims an untested guarantee.
Let us consider is mistaken for reader agreement or permission to execute a task.
exceptions: Clear operational instructions can appropriately use direct imperatives.
A stipulated hypothetical may be explored without pretending it is an observed fact.
Sparing use is a contextual craft judgment, not a ban on directive-rich manuals.

example.before: Draft: Add a label and every reader will identify the box correctly. Notes: A label is proposed to help identification; no user testing exists. Request: Diagnose the promise.
example.after: The directive proposes an action; “every reader will” adds an untested universal result. Keep the identification purpose separate from a guaranteed outcome. The lack of testing does not establish that labeling is ineffective.
example.why: Distinguishes forceful formulation from evidence of universal success.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: Labeling is proposed, not reported as completed.
Its purpose is to help identification.
No universal success or failure is established.
Do not perform the directive or invent test results.

alternatives.text: This sentence can invite labeling, but the result clause requires evidence beyond the instruction itself. A bounded claim about the intended help would be more faithful if revision is requested.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When identifying the exact overcommitment without rewriting.
alternatives.tradeoff: Leaves the final wording to the authorized editing mode.

counterexample.text: Draft: Place the label on the front of the box. Notes: This is the required procedure. Request: Proofread.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The instruction is clear. Do not weaken a required action into a tentative invitation merely because imperatives can sound forceful.

cards.title: Judge an exclamation by the emphasis it earns
cards.mechanism: Exclamatory syntax, a fragment or punctuation can carry urgency, relief or personal commitment. It need not include an exclamation mark, and a mark is not evidence of an actual emotion or a defect. Judge the supplied voice and context before flattening or amplifying the line.
steps: Identify the supported event and the voice’s intended emphasis.
Compare marked and restrained presentations only in the requested mode.
Keep an earned beat; do not add emotional claims or infer melodrama from punctuation alone.
triggers: Every exclamation mark is automatically removed as unprofessional.
An editor adds emotional punctuation where the brief calls for restrained reporting.
exceptions: Formal genres or explicit house styles may require restraint.
A narrative can carry emotion without overt exclamation.
Frequency and sentence length do not supply universal exclamation limits.

example.before: Draft: The latch held! Notes: In a fictional voice, this is the narrator’s intended moment of relief; the latch did hold. Request: Diagnose, not rewrite.
example.after: The exclamation gives the confirmed event its intended relieved beat. It is not a mechanics error or automatically melodramatic. A period would be more restrained, but this diagnosis task does not authorize flattening the supplied voice.
example.why: Checks the contextual job of emphasis without imposing a punctuation ban.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: The latch held.
Relief is supplied as the intended fictional voice effect.
No injury, danger, cause or duration is supplied.
Diagnosis only.

alternatives.text: The mark is defensible in this voice. Keep the factual event distinct from the expressive emphasis; a quieter ending is a craft option, not an obligatory correction.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the user asks whether the punctuation itself is wrong.
alternatives.tradeoff: Does not claim all repeated exclamations work equally well.

counterexample.text: Brief: A restrained maintenance log, without expressive punctuation. Draft: The latch held! Request: Proofread against that format.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The explicit format constraint warrants removing expressive punctuation while preserving the event; do not insist that the fictional treatment applies to this log.

cards.title: Omit a repeated predicate only when its recovery stays faithful
cards.mechanism: Parallel structure can let the reader recover omitted words, producing concise ellipsis. Check the actual shared predicate, negation and qualifications; an attractive gap must not make different actions appear identical or erase a material limit.
steps: Expand the candidate ellipsis mentally to name the understood words.
Check that the recovered predicate and each item’s conditions match the supplied record.
Compare concise and explicit forms; keep explicit wording when recovery is materially ambiguous.
triggers: A repeated predicate can be omitted in a clear paired comparison.
An elliptical second item ambiguously inherits the first item’s action or negation.
exceptions: An audience or format may benefit from fully explicit clauses.
Poetic or literary ellipsis can be deliberately strained; do not impose it on operational prose.
Shared grammar does not mean equal evidence, identical quantities or interchangeable actors.

example.before: Draft: The east gate opens at nine; the west gate opens at ten. Notes confirm both opening times. Request: Compress lightly without adding a time convention.
example.after: The east gate opens at nine; the west gate at ten.
example.why: The second clause recoverably shares opens while retaining the distinct gates and times.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: The east gate opens at nine.
The west gate opens at ten.
No AM/PM, date, closure time or reason is supplied.

alternatives.text: The east gate opens at nine; the west gate, at ten.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a visual pause helps the audience recover the missing predicate.
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds marked punctuation; the comma is a stylistic option, not a universal requirement.

counterexample.text: Notes: Mara approved the report, but Noel only reviewed the budget. Candidate: Mara approved the report; Noel the budget.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The gap transfers approved to Noel and changes his action. Retain reviewed and its qualification rather than forcing parallel ellipsis.

cards.title: Distinguish a deliberate grammatical shift from a broken comparison
cards.mechanism: A coordinated series may depart from matching grammatical forms to sustain an informal voice or give one item separate weight. Recover the functions and meaning before enforcing symmetry; deliberate disruption is not a general license to obscure an operational comparison.
steps: Identify what each item says and how it participates in the series.
Check whether the grammatical shift contributes to the established voice or emphasis.
Compare a conventional alignment only if authorized; reject changes that remove a distinct behavior or invent a unifying cause.
triggers: A mixed adjective, noun phrase and participial phrase is automatically normalized.
An instruction’s mismatched forms make the required actions hard to recover.
exceptions: Formal lists may require parallel action forms.
Different grammatical forms can still do comparable descriptive work.
Deliberate syntax does not prove all semantic mismatches are intentional.

example.before: Draft: He was restless, a poor sleeper, and always arriving early. Notes: These are three intended descriptions in an informal fictional voice. Request: Diagnose, preserve useful irregularity.
example.after: The items use different forms but supply interpretable descriptions of the same person. The shift into ongoing behavior can earn emphasis in this informal voice. Do not call it a factual contradiction or normalize it solely for grammatical symmetry; assess any actual reading difficulty in context.
example.why: Preserves the three supplied descriptions without mistaking irregular shape for inconsistent content.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: He is restless.
He is a poor sleeper.
He habitually arrives early.
No causal explanation links these descriptions.
Diagnosis only.

alternatives.text: This is marked coordination, not necessarily failed meaning. A formally matched series is possible, but would change the supplied voice and may reduce the final behavior’s separate weight.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the formal-versus-informal tradeoff is the central craft issue.
alternatives.tradeoff: Does not pretend every grammatical mismatch is effective.

counterexample.text: Brief: Use parallel action instructions. Draft: Check the seal, dryness, and to attach the label. Request: Clarify the required steps using supplied notes.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The explicit format and unclear action on dryness justify a repair or a targeted question. Do not invoke literary disruption to avoid a real instruction problem.

cards.title: Let a supported turn break an established pattern
cards.mechanism: A repeated frame can prepare a final departure in syntax or meaning. That departure should express an actual distinction, not an invented climax; restoring surface symmetry can erase a turn from capability to commitment or from expectation to limitation.
steps: Identify the stable repeated frame and what the final unit changes.
Test that the new contrast is supported and genuinely advances the thought.
Preserve an earned departure or compare a plainer form; never manufacture stakes just to complete a pattern.
triggers: The last sentence breaks repeated can clauses to ask about willingness.
An editor repeats the opening pattern at the end and loses the intended turn.
exceptions: A list of equivalent facts may need stable repetition all the way through.
A climactic break is an option, not a required ending.
Capability does not establish willingness, obligation or a future action.

example.before: Draft: The crew can inspect the panel. It can measure the gap. It can record the result. The unresolved question is whether it will do the work. Notes: Ability is established; willingness is not. Request: Diagnose the final break.
example.after: The final sentence makes a supported turn from capability to willingness. It does not contradict the earlier can statements. Keep that distinction; a symmetrical ending that reports the work as done or inevitable would overstate the notes.
example.why: Explains the semantic turn without confusing available action with actual commitment.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: The crew has all three stated capabilities.
Its willingness to do the work remains unresolved.
No result, refusal or obligation is established.
Diagnosis only.

alternatives.text: The repeated capabilities prepare the last question rather than answer it. The break earns its place by changing the issue from what the crew can do to what it is willing to do.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When explaining paragraph movement and the final emphasis.
alternatives.tradeoff: Interprets the stated willingness frame; does not prescribe a new ending.

counterexample.text: Brief: A neutral inventory of three available capabilities; no decision about willingness is requested or supported.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not add a dramatic will-they turn merely to make the ending distinctive. The inventory can end plainly.

cards.title: Anchor directional links in the supplied viewpoint
cards.mechanism: Where, when and how frames can let a sequence cohere without extra transition words. Spatial pointers require a recoverable viewpoint; left or beyond should not silently switch observers, add a compass direction or promise identical mental images.
steps: Identify the observer, starting frame and supplied spatial relations.
Track whether the viewpoint stays fixed or a move is explicitly supplied.
Clarify a material reference gap within the task while retaining supported positions and uncertainty.
triggers: Left and right change their implied observer without a stated viewpoint shift.
Several scene locations are listed without the frame needed to connect them.
exceptions: A viewpoint shift can be deliberate and properly signaled.
Not every description needs a map, orientation sentence or exact distance.
An unverified external geography is not an internal contradiction.

example.before: Draft: The rack is to my left. The desk is to my right. Behind it is the hatch. Notes: The narrator observes from the doorway; it means the desk. Request: Clarify orientation without adding detail.
example.after: From the doorway, the rack is to my left and the desk is to my right. The hatch is behind the desk.
example.why: Adds only the supplied vantage and resolves the supplied referent of it.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: The observer is at the doorway.
The rack is to that observer’s left and the desk to the right.
The hatch is behind the desk.
No compass bearing, distance, motion or lighting is supplied.

alternatives.text: From the doorway, I see the rack to my left and the desk to my right, with the hatch behind the desk.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When one continuous observational sentence fits the surrounding voice.
alternatives.tradeoff: More cumulative; the original two-sentence repair makes the hatch relation easier to isolate.

counterexample.text: Draft: From the doorway, the rack is to my left. At the desk, looking back, it is to my right. Notes confirm the change of viewpoint.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The changed direction can follow from a supplied viewpoint shift. Do not impose a same-observer frame and allege contradiction automatically.

cards.title: Use a list without adding order, completeness or authority
cards.mechanism: Numbered or bulleted units can clarify comparable ideas, but layout can imply a sequence, hierarchy or exhaustive account absent from the material. Name the actual relation and retain conjecture or qualification across every item.
steps: Determine whether the items are steps, alternatives, causes, examples or priorities.
Choose a layout that supports scanning without implying unsupported ordering or completeness.
Keep the shared qualifier visible and check that every item still has the same evidential status.
triggers: Possible explanations become three definitive causes in a numbered list.
Bullets drop a conjecture qualifier or imply all options have been covered.
exceptions: Real ordered instructions should retain their required sequence.
Lists can be helpful in technical or scanned prose; they are not inherently authoritarian.
Continuous prose may better preserve a qualification or interdependence that a list obscures.

example.before: Draft: The delay may reflect the file format, queue load, or missing metadata. Notes: These are possible contributors, neither confirmed nor exhaustive; no order is established. Request: Make the possibilities easy to scan.
example.after:
Possible contributors to the delay:

- the file format
- queue load
- missing metadata

These are not confirmed or exhaustive.
example.why: Retains possibility and the supplied coverage limit without presenting a ranked or procedural sequence.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: All three supplied possibilities remain visible.
No contributor is confirmed.
The list is not exhaustive.
No priority or required testing order is established.

alternatives.text: Possible contributors—not a confirmed or exhaustive list—are the file format, queue load, and missing metadata.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a short sentence carries the shared qualifications more naturally than bullets.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less scannable, but keeps the uncertainty adjacent to the items.

counterexample.text: Procedure: First disconnect the unit; then remove the cover. Notes require that order. Request: Format as numbered steps.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The sequence is supplied and materially important. Do not erase numbering or flatten the steps into unordered alternatives.

cards.title: Let sentence movement reflect the supplied scene movement
cards.mechanism: Syntax can suggest repetition, interruption, acceleration, accumulation or subsiding action. Its effect is contextual, not a fixed symbol dictionary. Compare forms that retain the supplied scene rather than manufacturing an event or emotion to make the prose seem alive.
steps: Recover the actual actions, pauses and perspective from the text or notes.
Compare a continuous, segmented or cumulative arrangement when the requested mode permits.
Check each event and relation after the rhythm edit; distinguish perceived effects from certainty about authorial intention.
triggers: An authorized cadence edit asks for a stop-start scene to feel stop-start.
An editor adds dramatic actions or motives to justify more vivid syntax.
exceptions: The same syntactic pattern can carry different effects in different contexts.
Literal reports or logs may benefit from direct exposition rather than mimetic fragments.
No requirement exists to symbolize every scene or copy a source author’s mannerisms.

example.before: Draft: She tapped, paused, tapped again, and rested her hand. Notes confirm this sequence. Request: Compare a segmented cadence for fiction; add no events.
example.after: She tapped. A pause. Another tap. Then she rested her hand.
example.why: Creates separately perceived beats while retaining the exact supplied actions and pause.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode; compare a defensible alternative while preserving the supplied commitments.
invariants: One tap precedes a pause and a second tap.
She then rests her hand.
No third tap, sound quality, fear, hesitation motive or elapsed time is supplied.

alternatives.text: She tapped, paused, tapped again, and rested her hand.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a continuous observation better fits the paragraph.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less segmented, but already clear and faithful; no change remains defensible.

counterexample.text: Brief: An exact event log with supplied timestamps. Request: Proofread without stylistic recasting.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not replace the record with lyrical fragments, alter time relations or invent recurring beats. Scene-mimetic syntax is not compulsory.

cards.title: Test a sound pattern without changing the supported observation
cards.mechanism: Word length, repeated sounds and spacing can cooperate with syntax to suggest an effect. Evaluate the local pattern, not a universal ban on repeated suffixes or a claim that one consonant always causes one response; preserve supported diction and do not invent sounds for variation.
steps: Identify the repeated sound or word shape and its relation to the stated action or voice.
Compare a bounded alternative only if the pattern creates a material problem.
Retain exact observations, uncertainty and voice; describe likely text effects without claiming to have heard unsupplied audio.
triggers: Repeated -ing or -ly endings are criticized solely by count.
A sound-based rewrite replaces an observed click with an unsupported creak.
exceptions: Repetition can intentionally support recurrence or a patterned action.
An accidental echo may distract in context; no suffix count determines correctness.
Models can inspect text patterns but cannot claim an actual read-aloud session from text alone.

example.why: Keeps the observed sounds while treating a text-level rhythmic effect as contextual.

No creak, bang, volume or mechanical cause is supplied.
Separate beats are the intended presentation.
No audio was supplied or heard; diagnosis only.

alternatives.text: The echo can carry the repeated observation. A compact inventory is possible if editing is authorized, but a suffix or word-repetition quota is not a reason to change the record.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When distinguishing a legitimate alternate presentation from mandatory variation.

cards.title: Choose a conjunction for the relation the material supports
cards.mechanism: Coordination links units without making their relationship interchangeable. A change from and to so, for, but or yet can assert a result, explanation or contrast that the original does not establish; fluent linkage is not proof of causality.
steps: Identify each clause’s assertion and the relation supported by the passage.
Compare coordination, juxtaposition or an explicit relation only within the authorized mode.
Reject a connector that adds an unsupported cause, result, contrast or equivalence.
triggers: A neutral event link is polished into a causal explanation.
A contrast word is added although the context supplies no contrasting expectation.
exceptions: Context can legitimately support a causal or contrasting connector.
And can carry continuity or suggested sequence; it is not a context-free logical operator.
Grammatical coordination does not establish equal evidential weight or argument validity.

example.before: Draft: The lamps went out, and Daro stopped speaking. Notes: Both events occurred; their cause and order are not established. Request: Diagnose a proposed change to “so Daro stopped speaking.”

example.why: Distinguishes a connector’s new commitment from a stylistic preference.

Diagnosis only; do not invent a power fault or Daro’s motive.

alternatives.text: Both clauses can stand together without a stated cause. “So” would require evidence or author confirmation that the darkness led to the silence.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the causal commitment is the central issue.
alternatives.tradeoff: Narrower explanation; does not prescribe a punctuation style.

cards.title: Make inclusive choice explicit without turning it into a forced alternative
cards.mechanism: Paired coordination and an inclusive choice frame determine what combinations are allowed. Replacing and/or with either alone, or dropping a correlative partner, may change eligibility even when the new sentence sounds cleaner.

exceptions: Exact quotations, formulas and conventional technical labels may require their original slash.

Parallel surface forms are useful but do not require erasing a meaningful grammatical difference.

cards.title: Compare a series’ connectors and pauses by function, not by a universal ban
cards.mechanism: Juxtaposed units, sparse conjunctions and repeated conjunctions can create different pauses, accumulation or urgency. Those rhythmic effects depend on context; the punctuation or a polished final balance does not establish a causal explanation or resolve the underlying situation.

A clipped literary sequence is automatically made into a fully subordinated explanation.
exceptions: A controlled literary comma splice can be deliberate; a formal format may require conventional clause punctuation.
Sparse connections can slow a passage as well as hurry it.
Rhythmic closure is not logical proof or factual resolution.

cards.title: Test there and anticipatory it by their information function
cards.mechanism: Existential there and anticipatory it can postpone new information or a heavy subject until the reader has a frame. They are not inherently empty framing. Removal should preserve the claim and its useful disclosure, not obey a blanket start-with-the-subject rule.
steps: Distinguish existential there or anticipatory it from a location word or referential pronoun.
Identify the new entity or postponed clause and the preceding reader question.
Compare a direct-subject form only when it offers a material benefit without changing the assertion.
triggers: Every sentence beginning there is is flagged as weak.
Removing anticipatory it forces a heavy clause into an unhelpful opening.
exceptions: Empty framing can still be expendable.
A locative there or referential it has a different job.
An existential opening does not authorize inventing what exists or where.

cards.title: Keep agent and object roles intact under fronting or inversion
cards.mechanism: Fronted objects and inverted subjects can put a known setting or a contrasted element first and new information later. Read grammatical roles and context before labeling an unusual opening incoherent; normalizing word order must not reverse who acts on what or erase purposeful focus.
steps: Recover the verb, actor and affected object independently of their positions.
Identify the contrast, known frame or end focus served by the arrangement.
Offer a conventional order only if authorized and compare its emphasis while retaining roles.
triggers: A fronted noun is mistakenly treated as the actor.
A forceful inversion is normalized solely for sentence variety.
exceptions: An inversion can be unclear or mannered for its actual audience.
Attribution in a fronted report must remain visible.
No quota of inverted or subject-first sentences is justified by source frequency examples.

alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the tradeoff between emphasis and neutral flow matters.
alternatives.tradeoff: Acknowledges a possible register cost without declaring an error.

cards.title: Recheck actor and event relations when moving a free branch
cards.mechanism: A free modifier may fit before, inside or after a base clause grammatically while changing its likely attachment, emphasis or implied event order. Mobility is not semantic equivalence; use the supplied scene to compare positions.

Compare possible placements against the supplied sequence or overlap.
Reject a move that creates a competing attachment or changes a required relation; do not treat all participles as simultaneous.
triggers: A left branch is moved past another potential actor for smoother cadence.
Movable modifiers are assumed to have identical meanings in every position.
exceptions: Several placements may be equally faithful.
Position suggests readings but does not by itself prove a physical chronology.
An own-subject absolute differs from a subjectless branch.

cards.title: Reduce opening load without dropping the condition that governs the claim

Separate essential prerequisites from descriptive opening material.
Compare a clearer conditional or context-first arrangement without turning a necessary condition into a sufficient guarantee.
triggers: Several opening frames delay the operational claim.
A front-heavy sentence is shortened by cutting a material permission condition.
exceptions: A long opening can earn its delay through orientation, parallel organization or voice.
Keep a condition early when the reader must know it before acting.
Relocation alone does not resolve unclear scope or unsupported reasoning.

Some participles function as adjectives rather than event reports.

A story seed is treated as factual evidence for its invented world rule.
exceptions: Nonfiction cannot silently turn remembered or reported material into invented events.
A proposed connection can be weak; novelty alone is not narrative quality.
An author’s borrowed inspiration does not grant reproduction rights or prove its factual claims.

example.before: Seeds: a numbered coat-check ticket and a lost dream. Request: Give two original speculative premises; invention is authorized.
example.after: Fictional possibility: A cloakroom takes dreams instead of coats; its numbered ticket is all a sleeper has to reclaim one.
example.why: Makes the connection explicit and labels the invented world rule, without imitating the source’s plot.

invariants: Use the numbered-ticket and lost-dream seeds.
Fictional invention is explicitly authorized.
No real event or paranormal claim is established.

alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the missing owner rather than the rules of storage should drive the opening question.
alternatives.tradeoff: Introduces a new fictional disappearance; it is not supplied history.

cards.title: Ask why an available alternative is not taken
cards.mechanism: A situation can be vivid while leaving an apparently easier route unaddressed. Test what the character knows, can do and wants before treating the unused route as an inconsistency; people need not optimize every action.
steps: Identify the stated goal and the competing action available under the supplied scene rules.
Check access, time, knowledge and costs without inventing an obstacle or motive.
If the passage leaves the choice unexplained, ask a located question; reserve a violation verdict for incompatible commitments.
triggers: A character takes a costly route although a known easier route appears available.
A critic calls a missing reason a definite plot hole.
exceptions: Fear, habit, values or mistaken judgment can legitimately govern a choice when supported.
A merely conceivable route is not necessarily accessible or known.
A character’s nonoptimal action is not by itself a contradiction.

example.before: Supplied scene: Mara knows the rear entrance is unlocked and can reach it in a minute. She wants the folder inside. Draft: She spends an hour sawing the front padlock. Request: Diagnose; do not rewrite.
example.after: The scene leaves Mara’s choice unexplained: she knows a quicker entrance is available. Why does she avoid it? This is a motivation question, not yet a physical contradiction; no supplied fact establishes a reason.
example.why: Tests a counter-route without assuming an optimal character or adding a rescuing obstacle.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode, compare an alternative and preserve the supplied invariants.
invariants: Mara knows the rear entrance is unlocked.
She can reach it in a minute.
She wants the folder inside.
No reason for choosing the front entrance is supplied.
Diagnosis only; no rewritten scene.

alternatives.text: Check whether the passage establishes a reason to prefer the front entrance. If it does not, flag the unused rear route as a pressure point without inventing danger or calling the action impossible.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a diagnostic should distinguish available action from a missing preference.
alternatives.tradeoff: Offers a check rather than deciding which fictional event the writer must choose.

counterexample.text: Supplied scene: The rear entrance is locked and Mara has no key. The critic proposes simply using it.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Reject the proposed shortcut because it violates the supplied access constraint.

cards.title: Replace vague flourish with precision backed by notes
cards.mechanism: An editor can remove redundant self-display and replace an indirect historical reference with a concrete fact checked against the writer’s notes. Precision earns its place through support and reader function, not through a universal ban on colorful phrasing.
steps: Identify the information the reader needs and the supplied record that supports it.
Compare a direct version and a fuller contextual version; remove only detail that does not serve this task.
Preserve dates, agency, qualifications and useful voice; ask for a missing fact rather than invent precision.
triggers: A report uses an atmospheric era label although the actual date is supplied in notes.
An edit cuts flourish but accidentally removes the record or qualification.
exceptions: An era label can be meaningful context rather than clutter.
Direct quotations require quotation-preserving treatment, not silent editing.
No supplied date means no license to invent an exact year.

example.before: Notes: The hall record was set in 2011 and broken Tuesday. Draft: In a truly astonishing feat, the record from those old factory days finally fell on Tuesday. Request: Light edit for a brief report.
example.after: The hall record, set in 2011, was broken Tuesday.
example.why: Uses the supplied date and event while removing unsupported praise and an unhelpful era label.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode, compare an alternative and preserve the supplied invariants.
invariants: The record belongs to the hall.
It was set in 2011.
It was broken Tuesday.
No performer or score is supplied.

alternatives.text: Tuesday’s performance broke the hall record set in 2011.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the new event rather than the existing record should lead.
alternatives.tradeoff: Shifts the information focus without specifying an unnamed performer.

counterexample.text: An oral-history quotation uses “the old factory days,” and the task is to preserve the quotation exactly.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Keep the quotation; add separately attributed context only if supplied and authorized.

cards.title: Test a poetic image’s function before applying literal-world criticism
cards.mechanism: An unusual image can carry a coherent idea without being a literal event. Consider the supported figurative relationship, the reader’s available context and competing interpretations; neither author intent nor unusual diction proves success.
steps: Establish genre and distinguish a proposed image from a literal assertion.
Test how the image relates to nearby pressure, movement or meaning rather than demand a single paraphrase.
Preserve a defensible image in analysis-only mode; ask about missing connections without inventing the poet’s intention.
triggers: A poem’s personification is called physically impossible by a literal scene checker.
A poet’s explanation is treated as proof that every reader can recover the same meaning.
exceptions: Literal reporting and technical instructions may require correction of an unintended agent.
Productive ambiguity need not collapse into one paraphrase.
A decorative or unsupported image can still fail; figurative permission is not immunity from critique.

example.before: Poem context: The speaker waits for news about a move. Line: Tomorrow keeps its coat on in my kitchen. Request: Analyze without rewriting.
example.after: “Tomorrow” is personified as a visitor not yet settled. In the supplied waiting context, the coat can sustain the uncertainty about staying or leaving. That is a defensible reading, not a claim about the poet’s private intent or a literal physical error.
example.why: Evaluates the image’s relation to context while refusing an automatic literal-error verdict.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode, compare an alternative and preserve the supplied invariants.
invariants: The text is a poem about waiting for news of a move.
Analysis only; preserve the line.
No private author intent or universal reader response is supplied.

alternatives.text: The image can keep the anticipated move unresolved: the visitor’s coat suggests either arrival or departure. Preserve that ambiguity if it serves the poem, rather than force a single explanation.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the writer wants to retain both possible directions of the image.
alternatives.tradeoff: More interpretive emphasis; does not establish that every reader will recover both possibilities.

counterexample.text: A maintenance report says “Tomorrow removed the valve,” but the supplied notes say technician Ellis removed it today.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not use poetic license to defend the report’s wrong agent and time.

cards.title: Reconsider an initial character label against the actual conduct
cards.mechanism: A writer’s first impression of a character may be as limited as a reader’s. Later conduct, another reader’s question or supplied contextual knowledge can challenge an initial label without establishing a hidden motive or a clinical explanation.
steps: Separate the initial label from observable acts and attributed accounts.
Compare plausible interpretations using the supplied conduct; keep uncertainty where competing readings remain.
Ask what context would resolve the distinction; do not assume sympathy requires liking the character or invent a diagnosis.
triggers: A quiet character is called passive despite initiating a consequential act.
An author’s dislike is treated as proof that a character has no workable perspective.
exceptions: Quiet behavior can be deliberate characterization rather than a defect.
Understanding a character does not require approving or liking them.
Author-supplied intention is relevant context, not proof that the page achieves it.

example.before: Supplied scene: Noor says little, but leaves first to warn a neighbor. Feedback: Noor is passive because she is quiet. Request: Assess the feedback, not the prose.
example.after: Quietness alone does not establish passivity: Noor initiates a warning. Her motive is still unspecified, but the supplied action challenges the label. Assess what she changes in the scene before deciding whether her characterization needs repair.
example.why: Uses the supplied action to test an initial judgment rather than inventing psychological certainty.

practice.task: Apply the requested mode, compare an alternative and preserve the supplied invariants.
invariants: Noor says little.
She leaves first to warn a neighbor.
No motive is supplied.
The request assesses feedback, not a rewritten scene.

alternatives.text: Distinguish reserved speech from inactive conduct. The warning gives Noor agency; whether it serves duty, fear or another motive remains a question, not an established fact.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the critique needs to separate behavior from possible motivations.
alternatives.tradeoff: Names interpretive possibilities without choosing one or diagnosing Noor.

counterexample.text: Supplied scene: Noor does not act and says she is choosing not to intervene. The writer wants to preserve that refusal.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not force a warning or another action merely to make the character more conventionally active.

cards.title: Do not turn a difficult creative period into a causal requirement
cards.mechanism: Work completed during suffering does not by itself establish that suffering caused or was necessary for the work. An author’s account of creative cost can challenge a romantic rule without becoming a universal clinical claim or a mandatory routine.
steps: Separate the reported work and circumstances from the asserted causal or necessary relation.
Check whether the supplied evidence supports only coexistence, contribution or necessity.
Keep the supported experience while narrowing an unsupported generalization; do not diagnose a writer or prescribe a health intervention from a memoir.
triggers: An essay says exhaustion is necessary for creativity because a novel was finished during sleepless months.
A famous writer’s difficult history is used as a mandatory creative routine.
exceptions: Supplied evidence can support a narrower causal claim; inspect it rather than automatically deny all influence.
An individual may report their own experience without claiming it applies to every writer.
The book’s autobiographical and clinical generalizations are not current medical evidence.

example.before: Supplied experience: I finished the novel during months when I slept poorly. Draft: Those sleepless months prove that exhaustion is necessary for good writing. Request: Edit the claim without changing the experience.
example.after: I finished the novel during months when I slept poorly. That experience alone does not show that exhaustion was necessary for the writing.
example.why: Retains the supplied experience while removing an unsupported necessity claim.

invariants: The novel was finished during months of poor sleep.
No causal comparison or necessity evidence is supplied.
No clinical diagnosis or treatment request is supplied.

alternatives.text: The novel was finished during a period of poor sleep; whether exhaustion helped, hindered or had no decisive role is not established by that fact alone.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the task calls for an explicit distinction between coexistence and possible influence.
alternatives.tradeoff: More analytical; preserves uncertainty rather than deciding the cause.

counterexample.text: A personal account says only: I kept writing during a difficult period. It makes no causal or universal claim.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Preserve the limited personal account rather than add an unsolicited refutation or medical explanation.

cards.title: Preserve shared scene constraints without forcing identical mental images
cards.mechanism: Readers may imagine unspecified surroundings differently while sharing the stated objects, relations and important marks. Select detail by its task function; a different mental image is not by itself a contradiction.
steps: Separate supplied scene facts from unspecified attributes and reader interpretations.
Compare sentence-level emphases that preserve the same scene constraints; do not present imagined attributes as established facts.
Use precision when consequences depend on it; test a rough comparison against the intended reader rather than assume identical visualization.
triggers: Two readers imagine a scene differently although its stated facts agree.
A request asks for grounded alternative perspectives without adding scene facts.
exceptions: Technical instructions can require exact measurements and materials.
Authorized fiction can invent details, but distinguish invented alternatives from faithful restatements.
A vivid communication metaphor does not establish telepathy or identical comprehension.

example.before: Supplied scene: A sealed envelope lies on a bench. It bears a red mark. Compare two sentence-level emphases without inventing facts.
example.after: On the bench lies a sealed envelope with a red mark.
example.why: Changes emphasis while preserving the stated objects, relation and mark, leaving material, size and motive unspecified.

practice.task: Compare two grounded emphases; identify shared constraints and unspecified details.
invariants: The envelope is sealed.
It lies on a bench.
It bears a red mark.
No material, size, motive or observer is supplied.

alternatives.text: The envelope bears a red mark and lies sealed on the bench.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the mark rather than the setting should lead the reader's attention.
alternatives.tradeoff: Brings the mark forward; does not establish its significance or origin.

counterexample.text: Supplied assembly instructions specify a 12-millimeter clearance; the dimension controls whether the part fits.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Preserve the exact supplied dimension rather than substitute an approximate scenic comparison.

cards.title: Keep a memoir's fragments and uncertainty visible
cards.mechanism: Selective remembered scenes can carry a narrative without a complete chronology. A remembered impression, another person's account and the present narrator's conjecture are different kinds of support; fluent connective prose must not silently resolve their gaps.
steps: Separate what the narrator remembers, what another person reports and what the narrator now guesses.
Retain supplied uncertainty about identity, date, sequence or motive while making the available scene legible.
Compare a fragment-led arrangement and a clearly attributed reconstruction; do not invent the missing connective event.
triggers: A memoir revision replaces perhaps or I do not remember with a definite childhood motive.
A writer wants a coherent recollection but lacks a continuous timeline.
exceptions: A fragmentary memoir can be intentional rather than a structural error.
Corroborated reconstruction is possible when its actual source is supplied.
Memory uncertainty does not automatically make the whole account false.

example.before: Supplied memory: I remember a yellow room. My aunt says we moved there when I was five. I do not know why we moved. Draft: At five, I moved into the yellow room because my mother wanted a fresh start.
example.after: I remember a yellow room. My aunt says we moved there when I was five; I do not know why.
example.why: Preserves the actual memory and attributed age while removing an unsupported motive.

invariants: The yellow room is remembered.

The reason for the move is unknown.

alternatives.text: My aunt dates the move to when I was five. What I remember is the yellow room, not why we came to it.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the contrast between chronology and personal memory is the governing point.
alternatives.tradeoff: More reflective ordering; does not independently authenticate the aunt's date.

counterexample.text: Supplied record: A dated letter says why the family moved, and the user wants an attributed reconstruction.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Use the provided corroboration rather than insist every recovered fact must remain unknowable.

cards.title: Turn a vague reaction into a located editorial question
cards.mechanism: A broad feeling about tone, mood or character becomes actionable when tied to a passage and an effect on understanding. It is feedback, not proof of defect; the next step may be a question rather than a rewrite.
steps: Ask which exact sentence or scene produced the reaction and what the reader understood or expected.
Classify the response as preference, blocked comprehension or a supported inconsistency.
Compare the intended effect with the observed response before prescribing a bounded change; respect the writer's choice about critique timing.
triggers: A critique says the tone is off but identifies no words or effect.
A workshop reaction is treated as a definite flaw without a recoverable reason.
exceptions: A reader can honestly report a reaction without having a complete explanation.
Early collaboration can be useful when the writer requests it.
A useful workshop or community need not fit one author's preferred private drafting routine.

example.before: Feedback: 'The scene feels wrong.' Request: Help me respond to the critique; do not change the scene.
example.after: Ask which moment felt wrong and whether the issue was unclear action, a character choice that seemed unsupported, or simply a different tonal preference. The general reaction alone does not identify a correction.
example.why: Finds the missing evidence without dismissing the reader or inventing an editorial defect.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Only a general reaction is supplied.
No passage-specific error has been established.
No rewrite is authorized.

alternatives.text: Ask the reader to quote the triggering sentence and describe what they expected next. Compare that expectation with the scene's intended effect.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the reader can identify a local reading experience.
alternatives.tradeoff: Narrower evidence request; may not capture a whole-scene response.

counterexample.text: Feedback quotes two incompatible dates for the same event and supplies the governing dated record.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not postpone an already located, supported inconsistency as though all criticism were vague taste.

cards.title: Prepare a truthful submission for the actual recipient
cards.mechanism: A brief professional presentation can help a recipient assess supplied work. Relevance and verifiable credits matter more than an old template; historical formats, agencies, fees and outcome stories do not establish current requirements or success.
steps: Identify the recipient's actual supplied or verified current guidelines and the task's permission boundary.
State the work, relevant fit and only supported credits/status; distinguish accepted, published, withdrawn and pending.
Keep unknown requirements explicit; do not invent an award, imply representation, contact anyone or pay a fee as part of drafting.
triggers: A query letter claims a story was published when it was accepted but never appeared.
A book's old postal template is treated as current submission policy.
An editor wants a polished professional letter but has not supplied credentials.
exceptions: The recipient can require more than a short cover letter.
Paid work and commercial goals are legitimate; an author's preference is not a moral ban.
A listed agent or encouraging reply is not proof of suitability or a guarantee of representation.

example.before: Supplied facts: 'North Window' was accepted by a journal that closed before publication. Request: State that history accurately in a draft query.
example.after: 'North Window' was accepted for publication, but the journal closed before it appeared.
example.why: Separates acceptance from publication without manufacturing a credential or a rejection.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The story was accepted.
The journal closed before publication.
No publication, award or representation is established.

alternatives.text: The journal accepted 'North Window'; its closure prevented the story's publication.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the interruption of the publication process is the focus.
alternatives.tradeoff: More explicit causal phrasing, supported by the supplied facts.

counterexample.text: Current supplied guidelines ask for a synopsis, sample chapters and a particular online form.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Follow the actual guidelines rather than force the book's brief postal presentation.

cards.title: Separate knowledge in the scene from knowledge acquired later
cards.mechanism: Retrospective narration can combine remembered perception with later testimony. Readers need to know whose information it is and when it became available; the narrator's later knowledge does not automatically belong to the experiencing character.
steps: Map the event time, the time the narrator learned each fact and the source of that fact.
Keep a later recollection or report explicitly framed when the scene would otherwise imply immediate knowledge.
Compare immersion and retrospective orientation without banning hindsight, guessing a motive or repairing missing memory with invention.
triggers: A memoir scene makes the narrator know another person's reason before they learned it.
A scene checker calls hindsight a contradiction even though it is clearly marked as learned later.
exceptions: A retrospective narrator may state later knowledge before describing the event if its frame is clear.
A supplied quotation or record can support another person's account, not necessarily independent confirmation.
A gap in memory does not authorize a made-up transition.

example.before: Supplied facts: I saw the driver beside the stalled van. A week later he told me he had been looking for a lost address. Draft: I saw him beside the van and knew he was looking for a lost address.
example.after: I saw the driver beside the stalled van. A week later, he told me he had been looking for a lost address.
example.why: Preserves the observation and later account while removing unsupported knowledge at the scene.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The driver was seen beside the stalled van.
The explanation came a week later from the driver.
The explanation remains attributed, not independently confirmed.

alternatives.text: When I saw the driver beside the stalled van, I did not yet have his explanation. A week later, he said he had been looking for a lost address.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the limit of the narrator's knowledge needs emphasis.
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds explicit temporal orientation without inventing what the narrator thought.

counterexample.text: Retrospective opening: I learned a week later why he had stopped. That afternoon, I only saw the van.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The time layers are already clear; do not call the framing inconsistent or force strict chronological narration.

cards.title: Adapt the writing process to present capacity without prescribing recovery
cards.mechanism: A writer's difficult return to work can illustrate practical adaptation, support and changed output. It does not establish that persistence cures injury, that pain proves dedication, or that another person should repeat the same schedule.
steps: Identify the writing task and constraints the user actually supplies, without diagnosing their condition.
Offer a smaller, optional and reversible task or a practical organization adjustment within that capacity.
Preserve the option to pause; separate personal meaning from causal claims about health or guaranteed improvement.
triggers: A writer is pressured to reproduce a famous author's painful return to work.
A routine is presented as proof that writing will heal an injury.
A user needs a lighter writing task under a stated time limit.
exceptions: The writer may freely choose a demanding session; it is not mandatory for legitimacy.
Support and workspace adaptation do not make a family structure or partner a universal requirement.
A personal recovery account is not medical guidance or a guaranteed trajectory.

example.before: Request: I have ten minutes available today. Help me resume my essay without demanding a completed paragraph.
example.after: Use the ten minutes to reread one passage and note the next question it needs to answer. Drafting can wait; the session does not need a word-count target.
example.why: Fits the supplied writing capacity without inventing a health benefit or promising a completed section.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Only ten minutes are available.
No completed paragraph is required.
No medical outcome or productivity diagnosis is supplied.

alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a small composition experiment is more useful than rereading.
alternatives.tradeoff: Creates options but does not promise an essay section.

counterexample.text: Request: I have a working routine and enough time; outline a full revision session.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not impose reduced output or a recovery narrative when the user has not supplied that constraint.

cards.title: Use a reading list as a perspective, not proof of book knowledge
cards.mechanism: An author's selected favorites can suggest a range of reading, but the list reports that author's response at a historical moment. Mentioned books have not thereby been reviewed, retrieved or absorbed by the assistant.
steps: Identify whether the evidence is a reading recommendation, an excerpt or the actual reviewed source.
Tie any craft inference to available material and its caveats; ask for an excerpt when the requested technique is unsupported.
Do not claim complete knowledge of listed works, universal endorsement or present publication status from the list.
triggers: A booklist is mistaken for access to every book it names.
A guide's favorite novels are treated as a universal canon or current recommendations.
exceptions: A listed work can be discussed from separately supplied and reviewed evidence.
The author's personal list can be useful without being universal.
Historical unpublished labels and reading periods are not current publication facts.

example.before: Request: This guide names a novel. Tell me the exact technique used in its final paragraph; no paragraph or independently reviewed source is supplied.
example.after: The list establishes that the guide's author valued the novel, not what its final paragraph does. Supply that paragraph or a source we can inspect before making a passage-specific claim.
example.why: Prevents a reference list from becoming invented passage knowledge.

invariants: Only the title's presence on a reading list is established.
No final paragraph is available.
No technique or current publication status is verified.

alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the goal is practice rather than an immediate passage-specific answer.
alternatives.tradeoff: Offers a next method, not the unavailable analysis.

counterexample.text: The user supplies the final paragraph and asks for a bounded craft analysis.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Analyze the available passage rather than refuse merely because the full novel has not been read.

cards.title: Adapt practice to the writer, not the writer to an author's quota
cards.mechanism: Regular reading and writing can support practice; a famous author's schedule is a candidate experiment, not proof of fixed talent or a condition for legitimate authorship.
steps: Identify the writer's actual time, access needs, obligations and goal.
Choose a feasible repeatable practice and a concrete way to notice useful progress.
Compare it with the author's routine without prescribing deprivation, substances, work beyond capacity or guaranteed success.
triggers: A writer is told that missing a daily word quota proves a lack of talent.
A beginner wants a writing routine but has only two short sessions a week.
exceptions: A word target can be helpful when freely chosen and compatible with the task.
A deadline, disability, care obligation or collaborative assignment can require a different routine.
Enjoyment, publication and output volume do not certify talent or improvement.

example.before: Request: I have twenty minutes on Tuesday and Saturday. Help me practice writing without a daily quota.
example.after: Use those two sessions: read a short passage and name one useful choice on Tuesday; draft a paragraph and test that choice on Saturday. Note what worked rather than demanding a daily word count.
example.why: Turns reading and practice into a feasible experiment without adopting an author's production schedule.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Only two twenty-minute sessions are available.
No daily quota is requested.
No promised publication or talent diagnosis.

alternatives.text: Use both sessions for the same paragraph: draft it on Tuesday, then read it aloud and compare two revisions on Saturday.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When continuity on a single passage matters more than a separate reading exercise.
alternatives.tradeoff: Narrower reading exposure, but a more visible revision comparison.

counterexample.text: Request: I already use a sustainable daily target; help me organize tomorrow's session.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not remove a voluntary working routine just because quotas are not universal.

cards.title: Explore a predicament through choices the characters can actually make
cards.mechanism: A situation can generate alternatives by combining goals, available knowledge, constraints and consequences. Discovery drafting is one option; the resulting branch still needs a coherent local world and explicit invention boundaries.
steps: Record the scene's fixed facts, character goals, available means and knowledge.
Compare plausible next actions and their costs; label newly proposed fictional conditions.
Do not force a desired ending through inaccessible information, unexplained rescue or a ban on outlines.
triggers: A fictional character solves a predicament using a fact they have not learned.
The user wants several grounded next moves from a scene rather than a predetermined ending.
exceptions: An outline can be a valid working tool; discovery is not the only method.
Uncertainty about a character's motive is not permission to invent it in nonfiction.
A proposal is not established story fact until the writer chooses it.

example.before: Fictional facts: Ivo is in a locked archive. He has a phone with no signal and hears a caretaker outside. Request: Compare possible next moves without adding equipment.
example.after: Ivo could call out, revealing his presence but seeking help, or stay quiet and listen, preserving concealment but delaying escape. Neither option tells him whether the caretaker is willing to help.
example.why: Branches follow the supplied means and knowledge rather than inventing a secret exit or rescuer.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The archive remains locked.
The phone has no signal.
A caretaker is audible; their intentions are unknown.
No new tool or exit is established.

alternatives.text: Compare the same two choices by urgency: calling out fits an immediate need to escape; waiting fits a stronger need not to be discovered. Ask which goal governs Ivo's choice.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the missing priority determines which action is plausible.
alternatives.tradeoff: Clarifies the decision but does not yet draft the next scene.

counterexample.text: Request: Keep my supplied scene outline and help the transition follow its established events.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not replace an authorized outline with compulsory improvisation.

cards.title: Select details that orient this scene without fabricating texture
cards.mechanism: A few functional sensory details can locate the reader and prepare action. Too little can leave a scene unreadable; too much can suspend the actual inquiry. The permission to invent in fiction does not transfer to factual prose.
steps: Identify the scene's immediate purpose, viewpoint and factual or fictional contract.
Select supplied details that orient location, action or attention; check what omission would obscure.
Compare a lean and a fuller arrangement, labeling any proposed fictional addition instead of manufacturing observation.
triggers: A scene lists every furnishing while the reader waits for the relevant action.
An editor adds smells, clothing or physical features not present in a factual account.
exceptions: A descriptive passage or later-relevant detail can legitimately take more space.
A remembered detail is not automatically verified because it feels vivid.
First visualized details and omission of appearance are process preferences, not universal rules.

example.before: Supplied observations: The lobby is dim. A green EXIT sign is above the door. Mara crosses to that door. Draft: The dim lobby contained many furnishings, which I have not recorded, as Mara crossed it.
example.after: The lobby was dim. Beneath the green EXIT sign, Mara crossed to the door.
example.why: Uses only supplied visible details to orient the destination; does not invent a decorative inventory.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Only the dim lobby, green sign and crossing are supplied.
No smell, furnishing, sound or emotion is added.

alternatives.text: Mara crossed the dim lobby to the door beneath the green EXIT sign.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When uninterrupted action matters more than pausing on the space.
alternatives.tradeoff: More compact; gives the setting less separate emphasis.

counterexample.text: Request: Describe the furnishings from my complete inventory for an accessibility planning report.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not cut task-relevant spatial detail as a storytelling digression.
