cards.title: Test what a comparison illuminates, not whether it is literal
cards.mechanism: A simile or metaphor earns its place by making a relevant relation perceptible. An unusual comparison can work under its context; obscurity and familiarity are questions of function, not evidence that the writer is ignorant.
steps: Identify the compared things and the shared quality supported by the sentence or scene.
Test whether the comparison makes that quality clearer or adds a useful comic or tonal effect.
Compare retaining, clarifying or removing it; keep figurative meaning distinct from factual mechanism or universal audience response.
triggers: A simile's shared quality cannot be recovered from the passage.
A metaphor is criticized as a physical impossibility without checking its figurative frame.
exceptions: A comic or surreal comparison can intentionally make an odd association.
Familiar language may fit a speaker's voice or a functional instruction.
A critic's failure to find a connection does not establish that no defensible connection exists.

example.before: Context: A single lamp gives unsteady light in a large dark room. Draft: The lamp flickered like a brave accountant.
example.after: The lamp flickered in the large dark room.
example.why: The accountant comparison supplies no recoverable relation in this context; removal retains the observation rather than adding a new image as fact.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: One lamp gives unsteady light.
The room is large and dark.
No character trait or new light source is supplied.

alternatives.text: In the large dark room, the lamp's light was unsteady.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When steadiness, rather than the lamp as actor, is the focus.
alternatives.tradeoff: Plainer rhythm without a figurative comparison.

counterexample.text: Comic context: The 'brave accountant' image has already been established as someone holding a wavering torch over impossible sums.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The supplied context can earn the unusual comparison; do not reject it simply for being unconventional.

cards.title: Let dialogue be an exchange, not a disguised information dump
cards.mechanism: Dialogue can reveal what speakers seek, assume, evade or misunderstand. Ear-tested choices need the actual situation and voice; dialect, profanity or polished speech alone do not diagnose intelligence, education or honesty.
steps: Identify each speaker's available knowledge, purpose and relation to the other.
Check whether the turn responds to the exchange or merely delivers exposition to the reader.
Compare a situational variant while preserving supplied voice and content boundaries; do not manufacture recorded speech.
triggers: Two characters explain facts they both know solely for the reader.
An editor adds slang or profanity to make every character sound human.
A nonstandard phrase is treated as proof of low intelligence.
exceptions: Formal or stylized dialogue can be intentional and genre-appropriate.
A character may genuinely use mild language; profanity is not compulsory realism.
Fictional dialogue can be proposed under permission; real quotations require the actual source.

example.before: Fictional context: Both siblings know the bus leaves at six. One is still packing. Draft: 'As you know, our bus departs at six o'clock,' Ren said. Request: Offer a less expository line.
example.after: 'The bus leaves at six. Are you packed?' Ren said.
example.why: Uses the known deadline as immediate pressure and gives the other speaker a reason to respond.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The bus leaves at six.
Both siblings know the departure time.
The other sibling is still packing.
No new motive or relationship history is supplied.

alternatives.text: 'Are you packed? The bus leaves at six,' Ren said.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the unfinished task should lead the turn.
alternatives.tradeoff: Shifts emphasis from deadline to readiness.

counterexample.text: Request: Preserve the stylized dialogue in this historical stage scene; proofread only.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not turn intentionally formal dialogue into casual contemporary talk.

cards.title: Compare a character's self-account with observable conduct
cards.mechanism: A role label is thinner than a person with aims and a point of view. A character's justification can explain conduct without endorsing it; an observed gesture alone cannot establish motive, moral identity or medical diagnosis.
steps: Separate supplied conduct, explicit self-account and narrator interpretation.
Compare supported perspectives and identify what remains unknown.
Propose fictional alternatives conditionally; do not import a diagnosis or treat sympathy as proof of innocence.
triggers: A character is only labeled villain, best friend or saint.
A scene's body language is used to assert a specific mental-health diagnosis.
The user wants two possible grounded interpretations of the same action.
exceptions: An explanatory label or summary can be efficient when the task requires it.
Different perspectives need not be equally supported; preserve what the passage actually establishes.
Understanding a justification does not endorse the action.

example.before: Supplied scene: Ena pockets the spare key and says, 'It will be safer with me.' No reason for her belief is given. Request: Analyze possible motives; do not rewrite.
example.after: Ena explicitly presents the act as protection. The same act could also serve control, but the scene does not establish that motive. Ask what access the others need and why she considers her custody safer.
example.why: Distinguishes her stated account from an alternate inference without inventing a hidden plan.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Ena pockets the spare key.
She says it will be safer with her.
No supported motive beyond her stated account is available.
Analysis does not authorize rewriting.

alternatives.text: Keep the protective statement as evidence of Ena's self-account, not proof that she is right. A later scene could test the account through how she responds when someone needs the key.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When planning a way for fictional evidence to develop.
alternatives.tradeoff: Suggests a future test, explicitly not an event that has already happened.

counterexample.text: Supplied passage: Ena explains that she is carrying the key to the agreed custodian, and the scene confirms that handoff.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not insist on a control motive after supplied evidence resolves the immediate action.

cards.title: Find a recurring concern without forcing a symbolic lesson
cards.mechanism: A second reading can reveal repeated objects, choices or questions that unify a piece. That supports a candidate interpretation, not proof of authorial intent, a mandatory moral, or the claim that every repeated detail is symbolic.
steps: Locate the actual recurring pattern and the scenes that give it significance.
Compare a supported reading with another plausible reading or a nonsymbolic function.
Strengthen only under revision permission; preserve productive uncertainty and genre exceptions, including deliberately theme-led work.
triggers: An editor demands a moral to close an unresolved narrative.
Repeated imagery is called intentional symbolism without supporting context.
The user wants to identify a draft's governing concern.
exceptions: A story need not contain symbolism to work.
Theme can remain a question rather than a solved lesson.
An allegory or deliberately theme-led project is not invalid because one author prefers discovery.

example.before: Supplied story: In three scenes, a shared key passes between neighbors. The last neighbor asks whether anyone will return it. Request: Name possible thematic concerns without adding an ending.
example.after: The repeated handoffs may organize a concern with trust or shared responsibility. The final question leaves that concern open; it does not require a moral saying that trust always fails.
example.why: Grounds interpretation in recurrence and uncertainty rather than imposing a lesson.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Three supplied scenes involve handoffs of a shared key.
The final question is unanswered.
No author's intent or universal lesson is established.

alternatives.text: Read the key first as a practical object whose circulation connects the scenes. Trust is a plausible thematic reading, but it need not be asserted as the only one.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When protecting against overinterpretation is more important than naming a theme.
alternatives.tradeoff: More cautious; leaves thematic synthesis to the writer.

counterexample.text: Request: Develop this explicitly allegorical story from my supplied thematic premise.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not forbid theme-first composition when it is the chosen form.

cards.title: Sort reader feedback by exact problem, not applause or vote count
cards.mechanism: A first reader can expose factual slips, blocked understanding and preferences. Agreement is a reason to investigate; taste, demographic fit and friendship do not establish semantic truth or oblige the writer to accept every proposed repair.
steps: Identify the feedback's exact passage, evidence and kind: factual, comprehension or preference.
Test the claimed problem against the draft and the actual audience; separate diagnosis from suggested repair.
Compare warranted changes and no-change choices while preserving the writer's purpose, deadline and permission boundaries.
triggers: Several readers dislike an ending but offer incompatible reasons.
A reader's correction is accepted without checking the source.
A guide's six-week rest or fixed draft count is imposed on a deadline task.
exceptions: An exact supported error can merit correction despite a split vote.
Repeated reader confusion can warrant investigation without making the readers' preferred rewrite compulsory.
Rest periods, friend readers and draft counts are personal process options.

example.before: Draft: The meeting was on Tuesday. Supplied calendar: Wednesday. Feedback: One reader flags the weekday; another wants a happier ending. Request: Diagnose, do not rewrite.
example.after: The weekday conflicts with the supplied calendar and needs correction if that calendar governs. The happier ending is a preference; evaluate it against the piece's purpose rather than treating it as a factual error.
example.why: Separates a checkable contradiction from a requested tonal change without editing under analysis permission.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The calendar says Wednesday.
The draft says Tuesday.
The ending preference supplies no factual correction.
No rewrite is authorized.

alternatives.text: Resolve the weekday against the governing record first. Discuss the ending separately: what effect does the writer intend, and what did the reader find unsatisfying?
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the calendar's authority or the ending's purpose needs confirmation.
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds explicit questions without manufacturing the resolution.

counterexample.text: Two readers prefer opposite rhythms, and neither identifies a meaning or comprehension problem.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not treat a tie in taste as an objective defect or compulsory change.

cards.title: Set pace by the reader's next need, not constant speed
cards.mechanism: Narrative pace can be fast or expansive. Cuts help when material adds no useful movement, but speed can also strip orientation, anticipation and character understanding. A percentage reduction is an author's heuristic, not a universal quality test.
steps: Identify what the reader is waiting to learn, feel or understand at this point.
Check whether the passage advances or prepares that need, and whether a cut would create a real gap.
Compare faster and slower arrangements under the selected genre; preserve necessary qualifications and material outcome.
triggers: Every reflective pause is cut because faster prose is assumed to be better.
A revision removes context solely to meet a ten-percent cut target.
A scene drags because the same question is explained repeatedly.
exceptions: A slower scene can earn its space through anticipation, reflection or orientation.
Reader interruption does not by itself prove boredom.
No fixed percentage cut establishes improvement.

example.before: Draft: The ferry was canceled. We waited by the gate. The gate was where we waited. Request: Tighten without losing the cause of the wait.
example.after: The ferry was canceled. We waited by the gate.
example.why: Removes only the repeated location assertion, keeping the event that makes the wait understandable.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The ferry was canceled.
The group waited by the gate.
No duration, weather or rescheduling is supplied.

alternatives.text: We waited by the gate after the ferry was canceled.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the waiting is the scene's immediate focus.
alternatives.tradeoff: Foregrounds the group; the cancellation becomes supporting context.

counterexample.text: A slow passage explains why the only available route is closed before the character chooses another.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not cut causal orientation just to accelerate the surface or hit a quota.

cards.title: Keep the result and participants legible without invented psychology
cards.mechanism: Event reporting can lose its subject behind rotating epithets, statistics and theatrical interpretation. Stable reference and selected decisive detail help readers understand what happened without pretending to know an athlete's mind.
steps: Identify the audience's need: a result report, technical analysis or a participant's perspective.
Keep names and key event/result details easy to follow; select statistics for the actual question.
Separate observed performance, attributed experience and inferred motive; do not diagnose health or psychology from the action.
triggers: A game report repeatedly renames participants to avoid repeating their names.
A sports passage states why a player acted without an interview or other support.
exceptions: A specialist statistics report may legitimately foreground many numbers.
A supplied interview can support an attributed account of experience.
A columnist's opinion is different from a factual finding; neither requires turning people into caricatures.

example.before: Context: Noor defeated Vale 6-4, 6-2. Noor won the last three games. Draft: The ace crushed the veteran because he wanted revenge.
example.after: Noor defeated Vale 6-4, 6-2, winning the last three games.
example.why: Names and relevant sequence remain, while an unsupported revenge motive and an evaluative synonym disappear.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Noor is the winner and Vale the opponent.
The score remains 6-4, 6-2.
No revenge motive, age or interview is supplied.

alternatives.text: Noor won the final three games to finish a 6-4, 6-2 victory over Vale.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the finish is the report's main focus.
alternatives.tradeoff: Foregrounds the closing sequence instead of the complete result.

counterexample.text: Request: Compare every serve statistic in these two supplied match tables for a coaching analysis.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not cut relevant quantitative evidence because a general-interest sports column would use fewer statistics.

cards.title: Support a critical opinion with the feature that earns it
cards.mechanism: A judgment becomes useful when readers can see the work, the criterion and the observed feature behind it. Conviction is compatible with a bounded opinion; it does not turn taste, inferred intent or disputed reception into fact.
steps: Separate observation, interpretation, evaluative criterion and the critic's preference.
Give a specific supported feature and explain how it bears on the verdict, supplying only the context this audience needs.
Keep uncertainty, relevant alternate readings and spoiler boundaries; do not invent reception history or demand provocation for its own sake.
triggers: A critique labels a work dull or brilliant without a recoverable feature.
A writer's style is condemned from a single taste judgment presented as a universal error.
exceptions: An opinion need not be universally shared to be defensible.
Necessary uncertainty is not a last-minute evasion to remove.
A spoiler-free review and a full critical analysis permit different levels of plot disclosure.

example.before: Context: The film repeats the same doorway shot four times while the character waits. Draft: The film is boring and the director has no imagination.
example.after: For me, the four repeated doorway shots slow the waiting scene without adding new information.
example.why: The critique locates its judgment in a supplied formal feature and owns the response rather than diagnosing the director.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: There are four repeated doorway shots in the waiting scene.
The evaluation is the critic's response, not a universal fact.
No claim about the director's capacity or private motive is supported.

alternatives.text: The repeated doorway shot may make the wait feel prolonged; I found the fourth repetition less effective than the first.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When an alternate intended effect deserves explicit consideration.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less categorical, but distinguishes a possible function from the critic's response.

counterexample.text: A reader says: The fourth identical shot made the character's trapped routine vivid to me.
counterexample.why_not_apply: That is a defensible reading of the same feature, not an error to erase merely because another critic found it slow.

cards.title: Judge humor inside its comic frame and truth contract
cards.mechanism: Parody can borrow a recognizable form, exaggeration can expose incongruity, and pure nonsense can exist for enjoyment. Literal correction or an added explanation may kill the designed effect; a factual nonfiction frame still cannot hide fabricated events.
steps: Identify whether the request is factual reporting, personal humor, clearly labeled parody or pure nonsense.
Find the frame, target if any, surprise and timing; test whether an explanation or repeated joke adds anything.
Preserve deliberate impossibility under the local frame, but keep fictional invention distinguishable from factual allegations or attributed speech.
triggers: A comic passage is criticized because an impossible event is literally impossible.
A parody is followed by a sentence explaining the joke.
An editor insists every humorous piece must teach a serious lesson.
exceptions: Pure nonsense need not make a serious point.
A clearly labeled parody permits inventions its factual counterpart would not.
Humor is audience-dependent; not finding it funny does not prove a logical defect.

example.before: Clearly labeled office parody: The stapler applied for annual leave. The manager rejected it for being too attached to its work. This is funny because staplers attach things.
example.after: Office parody: The stapler applied for annual leave. The manager rejected it for being too attached to its work.
example.why: The impossible character and borrowed administrative form are intentional; the explanation repeats the punchline's work.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The passage is labeled parody, not actual office reporting.
The joke depends on attachment and the leave request.
No real person's quotation or misconduct is invented.

alternatives.text: Office parody: The stapler's leave request was denied: attachment to the job was listed as a performance requirement.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When bureaucratic diction is itself the comic vehicle.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less direct wordplay and a more institutional cadence.

counterexample.text: Nonsense verse: The moon wore socks and lost a shoe.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not demand an underlying social argument or repair the impossibility when the user has chosen nonsense.

cards.title: Preserve a voice's useful resonance without imposing one register
cards.mechanism: Plain concrete words, long shaped syntax and remembered cadences can coexist. A formal or vernacular voice can carry identity and shared associations; audience and task determine whether those associations help or obstruct.
steps: Identify the supplied voice, intended register and what the cadence or reference contributes.
Compare clearer variants without automatically replacing elevated language, dialect, repetition or a long controlled sentence.
Check actual audience access and source reuse; neither assume everyone shares an allusion nor invent the writer's heritage or lived experience.
triggers: An editor flattens deliberate ceremonial language into a terse notice.
A long, coherent sentence is labeled clutter solely because a simplicity guide prefers short sentences.
exceptions: Eloquence can use controlled long syntax; simplicity is not a sentence-length ceiling.
A dialect or casual phrase is not automatically careless or condescending.
An allusion can exclude readers who do not know it; a small orientation may help without erasing the voice.

example.before: Ceremonial draft: We remember the hands that laid these stones, the rooms they raised, and the neighbors those rooms sheltered.
example.after: We remember the hands that laid these stones, the rooms they raised, and the neighbors those rooms sheltered.
example.why: The parallel widening from labor to place to community is legible and purposeful; a brevity prescription offers no material reason to flatten it.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The passage commemorates construction and shelter.
No new history or cultural identity is invented.
Preserve the ceremonial purpose.

alternatives.text: We remember those who laid these stones and raised rooms to shelter their neighbors.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the occasion needs a briefer version.
alternatives.tradeoff: Retains the action and community but loses some cumulative cadence.

counterexample.text: Request: In a safety notice, state which exit is closed and give the usable route.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not import ceremonial resonance when the task needs direct, usable orientation.

cards.title: Turn an expert's compressed answer into the right follow-up question
cards.mechanism: Expert shorthand often leaves a novice's mechanism or condition unstated. An identified question is safer and more useful than a guessed explanation, and questions should change with the audience's actual purpose.
steps: Identify the audience and what the supplied answer explains versus assumes.
Ask a concrete why, how, what changes or what limit question that fills the relevant gap.
Do not pretend the follow-up was answered; distinguish obtaining an explanation from verifying the claim, and respect interview/communication boundaries.
triggers: An expert says the equipment does the rest but the audience needs to know what the operator still controls.
A profile's questions are reused unchanged for a technical how-to article.
exceptions: An unanswered question stays unanswered; do not supply an imagined expert reply.
A sincere question is not a credential or independent verification.
Contacting or interviewing someone requires authorization; planning a question is not performing the interview.

example.before: Source: The engineer says, 'The filter improves the image.' Request: Help a beginner understand what to ask next.
example.after: Ask what the filter changes in the image, under what conditions it helps, and what information it might remove. The supplied answer does not yet resolve those points.
example.why: The next questions target effect, conditions and tradeoff rather than inventing an optical mechanism.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: No filter mechanism or result beyond the supplied claim is known.
No interview has been performed.
Questions fit beginner understanding, not an expert's assumed vocabulary.

alternatives.text: Ask the engineer to compare the same scene with and without the filter and explain the visible differences.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a concrete demonstration is feasible.
alternatives.tradeoff: May reveal differences clearly, but one demonstration does not establish all operating conditions.

counterexample.text: The source already supplies a complete side-by-side explanation for the specified filter and conditions.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not insist every first answer is insufficient; assess the actual explanation and ask only for a real gap.

cards.title: Find a viable project frame before polishing every sentence
cards.mechanism: Scope, intention, perspective and form determine which material belongs. Several good stories may exceed one short article but fit a larger project; discovery exercises are choices, not commands to abandon deadlines or outlines.
steps: State the task's audience, form, length, deadline and central question.
Compare at least two viable frames using supplied material; identify what each includes, excludes and would need to support.
Recommend a fitting scope without pretending only one frame is legitimate; preserve the writer's chosen perspective and contractual boundaries.
triggers: A short piece tries to be memoir, social investigation and a complete historical account at once.
The user cannot choose between a childhood viewpoint and an adult retrospective voice.
exceptions: Several forms can fit a larger deliberately structured work.
A real deadline or prescribed assignment still matters.
Multiple perspectives can coexist when signaled; an exercise's no-drafting rule is not universal.

example.before: Request: Plan a 700-word piece using my school football memory, my present friendship with teammates, and my notes about changing school policy.
example.after: Two viable frames: a focused memoir of one shared match with a brief present-day coda, or a policy piece using the memory as an opening and the supplied policy notes as evidence. A full account of all three threads likely needs more space.
example.why: The options expose form and evidence obligations before sentence polishing, without declaring any thread intrinsically unworthy.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The requested length remains 700 words.
No policy finding or memory detail is invented.
The writer chooses the governing purpose.

alternatives.text: For 700 words, center the continuing friendship; use one match as its origin and omit the policy investigation unless it directly bears on that relationship.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the writer's main intention is to explore the friendship.
alternatives.tradeoff: Stronger unity but less room for institutional context.

counterexample.text: Request: Plan a book with distinct sections for childhood memoir, adult friendship and researched school policy.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not apply a short-article compression rule to a book that explicitly has room for the separate threads.

cards.title: Budget context and mark a genuine new stage
cards.mechanism: A long article needs both local sentence links and a larger map. Context earns space when it prepares the next needed understanding; a scene break can signal a real change without decorative transitions.
steps: Identify the piece's governing question and the reader's next needed fact.
Choose what context is necessary for that stage, preserving qualifications and not implying the writer researched what is unsupplied.
Use a heading, break, time cue or transition for a genuine shift; compare arrangements without imposing a fixed lead length or one-idea-per-sentence rule.
triggers: A long piece has clear sentences but an obscure sequence of sections.
Interesting background overwhelms the current narrative question.
A flashback begins without orienting the reader.
exceptions: Background that changes how evidence should be understood must not be cut as a detour.
A scholarly or explanatory audience can require more context than a magazine scene.
A signpost should correspond to a real change; a fixed lead length is not a source requirement.

example.before: Current scene: We arrive at the dock on Friday. Next paragraph: Three years earlier the ferry route closed for a month. Request: Orient readers without adding facts.
example.after:
We arrive at the dock on Friday.

Three years earlier, the ferry route had closed for a month.
example.why: A boundary and an early time cue make the retrospective stage visible without inventing a cause or scene.

invariants: The current arrival is Friday.
The earlier closure was three years before and lasted a month.
No causal link between the closure and arrival is supplied.

alternatives.text: Before describing Friday's arrival, explain the earlier closure: three years before, the ferry route had closed for a month.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the closure must prepare the reader's understanding of the arrival.
alternatives.tradeoff: Provides context sooner, but defers the current scene.

counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not cut that background to speed the narrative; it materially qualifies the comparison.

cards.title: End at the fulfilled question, not automatically at the final event
cards.mechanism: The experience's chronology and the written piece's destination can differ. A discovered climax or echo can close the actual inquiry, but selective ending must not conceal a later fact that changes the represented outcome.
steps: Identify what question or expectation the piece has established.
Compare the proposed ending with the strongest supported point of resolution and the narrator's established voice.
Cut only incidental aftermath; retain or disclose a later reversal that changes the story's factual meaning.
triggers: A piece continues through routine travel after its central encounter is resolved.
A conclusion repeats an explanation instead of ending on the supplied decisive moment.
exceptions: A later reversal that changes the represented outcome cannot be omitted to manufacture closure.
A practical report may need the final operational result rather than a resonant scene.
An ending can change during composition without making the earlier plan wrong.

example.before: Context: The essay asks whether I could finish the night watch. Draft: At dawn, the next keeper took the lantern. I walked home, washed the cup, and sorted the mail.
example.after: At dawn, the next keeper took the lantern.
example.why: The supplied handoff closes the watch; the routine aftermath adds no stated information to that question.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The watch reaches dawn and the next keeper takes the lantern.
No feeling of triumph or later outcome is invented.
Do not suppress later material that changes whether the watch was completed.

alternatives.text: The next keeper took the lantern at dawn.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the completed night's timing should carry the final emphasis.
alternatives.tradeoff: Moves the dawn cue to the end without adding an actor to the transfer.

counterexample.text: The report says the bridge reopened, but the supplied next-day inspection found it unsafe and closed it again.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Ending at the reopening would misrepresent the outcome; preserve the reversal.

cards.title: Negotiate a real repair without erasing the writer's point
cards.mechanism: An editor can improve access and spot inconsistencies while accidentally flattening cadence or altering belief. A good repair makes the actual problem explicit and preserves the writer's meaning, with justified no-change decisions.
steps: Name the exact access or fidelity problem, if any, rather than proving usefulness by tinkering.
Explain the function of deliberate repetition or register and compare minimal alternatives.
Preserve opinions, supplied nuance and mode; ask when the intended point cannot be recovered, and do not implement discussion-only choices as rewriting.
triggers: An editor substitutes synonyms for intentional repetition.
A clean sentence is rewritten simply to show that editing occurred.
A revision changes what the writer believes.
exceptions: A meaningful repeated word is not automatically redundancy.
Voice protection does not excuse an actual ambiguity that blocks understanding.
Analysis or selected discussion choices do not grant permission to edit.

example.before: Draft: We return to the shore because the shore is where the story began. Request: Proofread; preserve the repetition.
example.after: We return to the shore because the shore is where the story began.
example.why: The sentence is clear and the repeated shore creates the requested echo; a synonym would not correct a proofreading error.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The request is proofreading, not a stylistic rewrite.
Preserve the deliberate repeated shore.
No belief, fact or tone is replaced.

alternatives.text: No correction needed. The repeated shore is deliberate and keeps the ending tied to its opening.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the user wants a diagnostic explanation rather than a replacement passage.
alternatives.tradeoff: Discusses the text without changing it.

counterexample.text: The draft says 'she saw her' with two equally possible referents, and the intended one is not supplied.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Ask which person is meant; protecting voice does not justify guessing an identity or overlooking genuine ambiguity.

cards.title: Test a modifier's contribution, not its part of speech
cards.mechanism: A modifier can repeat an implication, add distinguishing information, calibrate evidence or supply purposeful voice. Deletion is useful only when its contribution is genuinely expendable.
steps: Identify what the modifier adds to the base assertion and the context.
Compare deletion and a more precise wording against the supported degree, uncertainty, contrast and tone.
Trim only within the requested editing boundary; do not replace a qualified claim with unsupported confidence.
triggers: A draft has redundant adverbs, decorative adjectives or timid-sounding qualifiers.
An editor proposes removing may, somewhat or approximately to sound authoritative.
exceptions: An evidential hedge is not a defect merely because it reduces confidence.
A familiar-looking adjective can distinguish an unexpected property.
Idiomatic emphasis, dialogue and deliberate repetition need not be literal measurement.

example.before: The siren shrieked loudly. The crack may be slightly wider than yesterday.
example.after: The siren shrieked. The crack may be slightly wider than yesterday.

invariants: The siren's loud sound remains.
A wider crack is possible, not established.
Any possible increase remains slight.

alternatives.text: The siren gave a shriek. The crack may be slightly wider than it was yesterday.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the comparison needs a more explicit time reference.
alternatives.tradeoff: A little longer but preserves the measurement's uncertainty.

counterexample.text: Only the pale-blue folders belong in the return bin.

cards.title: Recover supported action without inventing an actor
cards.mechanism: Visible actions can make a report easier to follow than stacked abstractions, but active voice does not license guessing agency or changing topic focus.

Test an active version if agency is known and relevant.
Keep an appropriate passive or abstraction when the actor is unknown, unimportant or not the sentence's topic.
triggers: A report hides a known action behind a noun chain.
A passive sentence is criticized without checking whether an agent is supplied.
exceptions: Unknown agents must remain unknown.
A passive can preserve the established topic or focus.
An abstract term can be the exact object of analysis, not evasive writing.

example.before: Context: The intake team reviewed the requests. Draft: Completion of request review was achieved by the intake team.

cards.title: Locate the reader before changing time, subject or stance
cards.mechanism: A small, early orientation signal can prevent a reader from carrying the preceding sentence's frame into a different one. The signal must express a real relation rather than paste on artificial logic.
steps: Track the reader's last known topic, time, viewpoint and expectation.
Locate a genuine shift and test an early contrast, time cue, named subject or revised order.
Ensure the connective does not invent a cause, chronology or opposition; preserve an effective implicit link.
triggers: A sentence changes time frame or direction only at its end.
A reader may attach a new description to the previous sentence's subject.
exceptions: A connective must not invent causation or opposition.
An implicit connection can already be clear.
Intentional suspense may delay orientation when the resulting reading is controlled.

example.before: Last year the clinic opened at eight. It opens at seven this year.
example.after: Last year the clinic opened at eight. This year it opens at seven.
example.why: The time shift arrives before the new opening time; no causal explanation is supplied.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Last year's opening time is eight.
This year's opening time is seven.
Do not invent a reason for the change.

alternatives.text: The clinic now opens at seven, rather than last year's eight.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the current schedule is the reader's main need.
alternatives.tradeoff: Condenses the comparison and changes its emphasis.

counterexample.text: The moon rose. Along the wall, the cats became visible.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The spatial connection is already intelligible; no automatic therefore or however is needed.

cards.title: Use paragraph boundaries for a unit of thought and reading scale
cards.mechanism: A paragraph is both a logical unit and a visual reading surface. Breaking every sentence apart can disrupt a developing thought; leaving every thought in one block can hide genuine turns.
steps: Identify the paragraph's developed point and any change of topic, time, evidence or action.
Test boundaries that keep dependent sentences together while exposing meaningful turns.
Consider the actual display and genre; avoid fixed sentence-count rules or inferring reader contempt from layout.
triggers: Closely dependent sentences have been split into a chain of tiny paragraphs.
A dense block contains a clear change from background to an instruction.
exceptions: A short paragraph can provide legitimate emphasis.
A long paragraph can remain coherent and readable.
Screen width and accessibility needs affect layout; paragraph length is not a verdict about the author's character.

example.before:
The gate remained locked.

The key was inside.

We waited for the caretaker.

By noon, the delivery had been cancelled.
example.after:
The gate remained locked. The key was inside. We waited for the caretaker.

By noon, the delivery had been cancelled.
example.why: The obstacle and response form one unit; the later outcome starts a new stage without implying why the delivery was cancelled.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The gate remains locked and the key is inside.
The group waits for the caretaker.
Cancellation occurs by noon, without an invented cause.

alternatives.text: The gate remained locked, with the key inside. We waited for the caretaker. By noon, the delivery had been cancelled.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When this compact account belongs in a single narrative paragraph.
alternatives.tradeoff: Smoother continuity but less visual emphasis on the later outcome.

counterexample.text:

Stop if you smell smoke.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Distinct action and safety condition can warrant separate short units; do not join them merely to satisfy a paragraph-length preference.

cards.title: Choose punctuation for the relationship and controlled pace
cards.mechanism: Periods, semicolons, colons, dashes and paired interruptions organize thought and pace differently. A guide's stylistic preference is not proof that one mark is obsolete or that long syntax is intrinsically wrong.
steps: Identify the relationship between clauses and any parenthetical interruption.
Compare permissible arrangements for hierarchy, emphasis and ease of following.
Preserve intentional syntax and the house convention; justify any change by its local effect rather than a ban.
triggers: An editor calls every semicolon old-fashioned or demands only short sentences.
A long sentence mixes independent stages without a controlled relationship.
exceptions: A semicolon or colon can be the clearest choice.
A controlled long sentence need not be split.
Expressive punctuation can be deliberate; do not impose a universal ban from historical taste.

example.before: The tide reached the steps, the rescue boat was still beyond the pier.
example.after: The tide reached the steps; the rescue boat was still beyond the pier.
example.why: The semicolon connects independent observations without inventing causation or making one subordinate to the other.

invariants: The tide reaches the steps.
The rescue boat is still beyond the pier.
No causal relation or rescue outcome is added.

alternatives.text: The tide reached the steps. The rescue boat was still beyond the pier.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When two discrete beats suit the intended pace.
alternatives.tradeoff: More separation and less overt balance.

cards.title: Remove irrelevant exclusion without changing the referent
cards.mechanism: A general statement can accidentally narrow a role to one group. Revising its reference can improve accuracy and access, but cannot silently change a specific person's identity, a quotation, or the quantifier's scope.
steps: Determine whether the reference is a general category, a particular person or a quotation.
Use a supported neutral role, plural, direct address or other suitable construction without changing who must do what.
Respect supplied identities and house requirements; consult current evidence for disputed usage instead of freezing the edition's prescriptions.
triggers: A general instruction assumes every participant has the same gender.
A rewrite changes singular duties into a collective duty while neutralizing a pronoun.
exceptions: A specific person's supplied identity and pronouns should not be silently replaced.
A quotation must not be silently modernized.
Pluralization can alter scope; preserve each person's individual obligation.

example.before: Every volunteer must submit his own timesheet.
example.after: All volunteers must submit their own timesheets.
example.why: The instruction still requires an individual timesheet from every volunteer without assigning gender to the role.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Every volunteer must submit a timesheet.
The obligation remains individual, not one shared sheet.

alternatives.text: Each volunteer must submit an individual timesheet.

alternatives.tradeoff: Less conversational, but makes scope explicit.

cards.title: Let supported particulars carry interest without added spectacle
cards.mechanism: A relevant concrete fact can engage readers more directly than a manufactured teaser or an instruction about what they should feel. Selection and context still matter; facts are not automatically self-explanatory.
steps: Find the supplied particular that bears on the piece's actual subject.
Bring it into view and remove only theatrical scaffolding or interpretation that does no needed work.
Keep explanation when readers need scale, stakes or technical context; do not invent a colorful scene.
triggers: An opening delays the actual event behind vague drama.
A report tells readers something is astounding but never shows the supplied fact.
exceptions: Readers may need an explanation of scale or significance.
A reflective narrator can intentionally interpret an event.
A surprising fact still needs source support; vividness does not authenticate it.

cards.title: Distinguish literary arrangement from invented speech or time
cards.mechanism: Nonfiction can select and arrange recorded material, but a smoother scene can misrepresent when words were said, what they meant or whether an exchange occurred. The book describes disputed compression practices; those are not blanket authorization.
steps: Locate the source and context of each quotation, event and claimed viewpoint.
Keep attribution and actual meaning; identify any splicing, composite scene or chronology change.
Prefer separate quotations or transparent framing when compression would create a false exchange or event; ask rather than infer unsupplied speech or inner life.
triggers: An editor wants to join remarks from different days into one seamless interview.
A nonfiction scene invents dialogue or an interviewee's thoughts for narrative flow.
exceptions: Separate remarks must not be presented as a single exchange without support.
A source's approval of historical compression does not establish present editorial permission.
A clearly labeled fictional exercise has a different truth contract.

cards.title: Build a place from useful observations, not a cultural essence
cards.mechanism: Selected details and activity can distinguish a place and support a perspective. A sample of observed behavior cannot by itself establish an entire population's motives or national character.
steps: Separate supplied observation, attributed local account and the writer's interpretation.
Select details for the current narrative or informational purpose and compare more than one supported perspective.
Limit generalizations to the observed scope; preserve uncertainty and avoid invented sensory experience or stereotypes.
triggers: A place description substitutes quaint or charming for distinguishing details.
A writer turns a few observed people into a claim about everyone in a culture.
exceptions: A single observation does not prove a national trait.
A service guide may need ordinary facts that a literary travel essay can omit.
Subjective response is legitimate when owned by the speaker and supported, not presented as everyone's reaction.

cards.title: Select a memoir's window while preserving memory status
cards.mechanism: A focused portion of a life can acquire shape through remembered details and relationships. Composition may discover an organizing idea, but it cannot verify a half-remembered event or fill another person's inner life.
steps: Find the bounded period, relationship or question the writer wants to explore.
Use supplied details that bear on that focus and distinguish recollection, records, interpretation and uncertainty.
Arrange a window into the experience without inventing exact speech, forcing disclosure or converting remembered uncertainty into fact.
triggers: A memoir draft summarizes an entire life without an organizing focus.
A polished version invents an exact date, smell, quotation or motive absent from the writer's memory.
exceptions: Memoir construction is not permission to fabricate factual detail.
A writer need not disclose intimate or traumatic material to satisfy a vividness prescription.
Autobiography, an application or a complete life record may legitimately require broader scope.

cards.title: Explain a mechanism in prerequisite order
cards.mechanism: Readers can follow unfamiliar processes when each step supplies the prerequisite for the next. Accessible sequence must preserve mechanism, conditions and the difference between observation, inference and possible application.
steps: Identify the actual audience and the terms or stages it must understand first.
Order the supplied mechanism so objects, operations and conditions precede conclusions that depend on them.
Explain necessary technical terms without replacing them inaccurately; label hypotheses and applications, and do not import the book's historical science as current evidence.
triggers: A technical explanation uses a term before defining its role.
An effect appears before the operation needed to explain it.
exceptions: Expert readers may not need elementary definitions.
Analogy or a human anecdote cannot replace the actual mechanism.
Historical scientific examples illustrate exposition; they do not verify today's scientific or medical claims.

cards.title: Use a familiar analogy without transferring its false implications
cards.mechanism: A concrete comparison can make an unfamiliar process legible by mapping a particular relationship. It becomes misleading when the reader is invited to import unrelated properties or treat illustration as evidence.
steps: State the specific feature the analogy is meant to illuminate.
Compare the mapping with the supplied mechanism and retain the limits that matter.
Return to the actual process; do not use an engaging metaphor as proof or infer an inner intention from it.
triggers: A scientific explanation uses a familiar image but hides where the comparison stops.
A metaphor assigns intention or memory beyond what the described system supports.
exceptions: An analogy is not factual evidence for a mechanism.
Only the mapped relation transfers, not every property of the familiar object.
Specialist writing can prefer a precise definition to an analogy.

example.after: The queue is like a waiting room: jobs wait their turn, and the program processes one at a time. The jobs do not feel impatience.
example.why: The useful ordering relation stays; an unsupplied mental state is explicitly excluded for a novice explanation.

invariants: Jobs are stored and processed one at a time.
Jobs have no supplied feelings or intentions.
The analogy supplies access, not evidence.

alternatives.text: The queue stores jobs in order, and the program processes them one at a time.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the audience needs the mechanism rather than a figurative introduction.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less vivid but avoids importing a misleading mental model.

counterexample.text: In a comic personification: The queued jobs grumbled about the wait.
counterexample.why_not_apply: A clearly framed fictional or comic personification need not be condemned as a literal technical error.

cards.title: Translate institutional abstraction into a supported reader action
cards.mechanism: Institutional writing helps readers when it says who will do what, when, and what the reader needs to do. Plain language must not replace ambiguous policy with guessed promises or erase exact technical distinctions.
steps: Identify the message's supported actor, action, timing and reader obligation.
Replace unnecessary noun chains with an intelligible action or a bounded request for clarification.
Preserve official terms when their distinctions matter; do not invent dates, outcomes, contact routes or motives to sound human.
triggers: A customer notice announces an enhancement but never states the concrete change.
A bureaucratic sentence has several possible plain-language translations.
exceptions: Plain wording must not add an unsupported promise.
A term can carry a precise contractual or technical distinction.
Unclear prose does not prove laziness, vanity or dishonesty; diagnose the text rather than the person.

example.before: Context: From Tuesday, customers can submit returns through the online form; telephone returns remain available. Draft: Return-processing channel functionality will be augmented effective Tuesday.
example.after: From Tuesday, you can submit returns through the online form. Telephone returns will still be available.
example.why: The supported added option and retained option replace an abstraction without claiming faster refunds or removing existing access.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The online form is an additional option beginning Tuesday.
Telephone returns remain available.
No faster refund, new deadline or guarantee is promised.

alternatives.text: We are adding an online returns form Tuesday. You can still request a return by telephone.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the institution's responsibility should be visible.
alternatives.tradeoff: Foregrounds the organization rather than beginning with the customer.

counterexample.text: Context: This technical specification distinguishes throughput capacity from latency. Draft: Capacity is 80 requests per second; median latency is 40 milliseconds.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not translate distinct technical quantities into a vague promise that the system is fast.

cards.title: Audit what a polished revision quietly adds
cards.mechanism: Rearrangement and rhythm can improve a paragraph while quietly adding examples, strengthening a claim or changing attribution. The polished draft must be checked against the actual source rather than presumed faithful because it reads well.
steps: Compare the original and candidate for new specifics, scope, certainty, motives and event relations.
Keep useful ordering and orientation changes while removing unsupported additions.
Allow more than one defensible arrangement; in diagnosis-only mode identify the tradeoff rather than applying a rewrite.
triggers: A fluent revision adds concrete examples absent from the original.
An editor changes remembered or possible information into a confident general claim.
exceptions: Improved cadence does not establish factual fidelity.
New content can be drafted if explicitly authorized and clearly labeled as hypothetical or fictional.
The source's sample revision is one arrangement, not the only correct one.

example.before: Original: I wondered whether the neighbors were too busy to visit. Candidate: The neighbors spent every evening watching television and had no time for friendship.
example.after: I wondered whether the neighbors were too busy to visit.
example.why: The candidate invents a habit, universal timing and a definitive motive. Restoring the actual question is preferable to elegant unsupported specificity.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The neighbors' actual motive is unknown.
No television habit is supplied.
The thought remains a question, not a finding.

alternatives.text: Were the neighbors too busy to visit? I could not tell.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the author's uncertainty should be more explicit and the change is authorized.
alternatives.tradeoff: Changes the sentence form but retains the question's unresolved status.

counterexample.text: Context: The user supplies a log showing the neighbors watched television every evening and asks to include that verified detail.
counterexample.why_not_apply: An authorized supported addition is not invention; check its source and scope instead of banning all new wording.

cards.title: Choose a useful process rather than enforcing an author's routine
cards.mechanism: Writers can arrive at effective prose by different working methods. Distinguish the output obligation from a personal process preference, especially when guides prescribe conflicting routines.
steps: Identify the actual obstacle and what the writer wants to produce.
Offer a bounded experiment compatible with the writer's constraints instead of prescribing a daily schedule, no-draft rule or required environment.
Judge the experiment by whether it helps the requested writing; preserve useful routines and do not diagnose the writer's personality.
triggers: The user asks whether rough drafting, outlining or revising one sentence at a time is the correct way to write.
Two sources' personal composing habits conflict.
exceptions: A process can be useful for one writer and obstructive for another.
A contractual deadline or required format remains binding even when the process is flexible.
Do not dismiss accessibility needs or medical difficulties as lack of discipline.

example.before: Request: I produce ideas in a quick rough draft. Should I stop because another guide says to perfect each sentence first?
example.after: Keep rough drafting if it helps you discover the material. Test sentence-by-sentence revision on one paragraph afterward and compare whether it improves clarity without stopping discovery.
example.why: The two routines become testable choices, not a hierarchy of supposedly legitimate writers.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Respect the user's existing productive practice.
Offer an experiment rather than a mandatory routine.

alternatives.text: Try drafting one short section more slowly, then compare it with your usual rough-draft-and-revise process.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the writer wants to test the alternative at composition rather than afterward.
alternatives.tradeoff: May improve local control but can interrupt generative momentum.

counterexample.text: I need dictation because typing causes pain; it works well for my drafting.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Do not prescribe abandoning an accessibility aid to follow a source's preferred writing instrument.

cards.title: Test a suspected cut without erasing the original
cards.mechanism: Marking candidate clutter and reading with and without it lets the writer test whether a deletion actually preserves meaning and improves the passage. The editor's first impression is a proposal, not authority.
steps: Identify the exact phrase and the job it may perform, including qualification, rhythm, contrast and interpersonal stance.
Compare the intact sentence with a temporary omission; check what commitment or implication changes.
Recommend the cut only if there is a material gain within the authorized mode; retain a reversible original and leave tied options to the writer.
triggers: An editor wants to remove a hedge or seemingly repeated phrase for concision.
The user wants a diagnostic before authorizing a rewrite.
exceptions: A hedge can be evidentially necessary rather than clutter.
A repeated idea may supply rhythm, orientation or contrast.
No fixed percentage-cut target applies; analysis alone does not authorize deletion.

example.before: The estimates are approximately roughly ten thousand dollars, assuming the roof needs no structural work.
example.after: The estimates are roughly ten thousand dollars, assuming the roof needs no structural work.
example.why: The doubled approximation can be trimmed, but the material condition and approximate status remain.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The figure remains approximate.
The estimate depends on no structural roof work.

alternatives.text: Assuming the roof needs no structural work, the estimates are roughly ten thousand dollars.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the assumption needs to be visible before the cost.
alternatives.tradeoff: Foregrounds the limitation while deferring the amount.

counterexample.text: The estimates may be lower if the roof needs no structural work.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Removing may or the condition would change the supported estimate; brevity does not justify certainty.

cards.title: Distinguish access to the thought from agreement with the voice
cards.mechanism: Readers need enough clarity to understand what the writer says, but an editor need not erase a writer's supported preferences, humor or perspective merely to please an imagined universal audience.
steps: Identify whether the difficulty is comprehension, missing orientation or merely a difference in taste or stance.
Repair genuine access problems while keeping the supported speaker relationship and distinctive choices.
Check the actual task's obligations: a personal essay and a public instruction have different responsibilities to their readers.
triggers: An editor proposes neutralizing a clear personal preference because some readers may disagree.
A direct factual message hides its key action behind an attempt to impress.
A passage is called wooden or brilliant without identifying a specific construction, reader effect or task.
exceptions: Audience needs and accessibility requirements cannot be waived by saying the writer writes only for themself.
First person is a tool, not a required insertion; do not fabricate personal experience or override a house style.
Do not infer incompetence, boredom or agreement from reader response alone.
Stylistic labels are provisional impressions, not mechanisms or diagnoses; name the observable effect and distinguish it from taste.

example.before: Draft: I prefer the rattling ferry to the silent tunnel. Request: Clarify without making me sound neutral.
example.after: I prefer the rattling ferry to the silent tunnel.
example.why: The clear preference is not a defect; disagreement by an imagined reader does not require editing it away.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: The speaker prefers the ferry.
Retain the supplied sound contrast.
Do not turn preference into a universal ranking.

alternatives.text: The tunnel is silent. I prefer the ferry's rattle.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a stronger contrast fits the surrounding cadence.
alternatives.tradeoff: Changes the rhythm and order without changing the preference.

counterexample.text: Public notice: 'Applications must arrive before noon Friday.'
counterexample.why_not_apply: Required deadline clarity and audience access govern this genre; the writer's personal taste cannot replace the instruction.

cards.title: Test what a familiar phrase commits the sentence to
cards.mechanism: A ready-made collocation can carry an unintended stance, event or causal picture. Inspect its actual contribution before replacing it, rather than rejecting familiar language or treating figurative wording as literal error automatically.
steps: Recover the sentence's actual claim and the stance or event implied by the phrase.
Compare that implication with the supplied facts, source attribution and genre.
Replace a mismatched collocation with supported wording; keep familiar idiom, irony or figurative compression when it is clear and functional.
triggers: Stock reporting language seems to import anger, delight, struggle or certainty not present in the record.
A guide's illustrative criticism treats a possible factual detail as impossible without checking its source.
exceptions: A familiar phrase is not automatically wrong or stale in every context.
An idiom need not literally describe its component words.
Do not refute an external factual claim merely because its evidence is absent from the excerpt; mark that dependency unverified.

example.before: Record: sales fell for three months; no attitude is recorded. Draft: The shop enjoyed a three-month decline in sales.
example.after: The shop's sales fell for three months.
example.why: The revision removes unsupported enjoyment while retaining the reported duration and direction.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Sales fell.
The period was three months.
Add no owner's attitude or cause.

alternatives.text: For three months, the shop's sales declined.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the duration belongs first in the paragraph's information order.
alternatives.tradeoff: Makes time rather than the shop the initial frame.

counterexample.text: She enjoyed the noisy debate and said so afterward.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Enjoyment is supplied and attributed here; deleting it just because enjoyed can be a stock verb would lose meaning.

cards.title: Treat historical usage judgments as evidence to assess, not timeless bans
cards.mechanism: Usage depends on sense, register, purpose and changing conventions. A guide's preference can prompt inspection without settling whether a construction is unacceptable for the user's present task.
steps: Identify the disputed word or construction and the specific meaning or register at issue.
Separate the source's historical taste from a present-day grammatical or semantic claim; consult an appropriate current primary reference when a consequential usage judgment needs verification.
Recommend the version that preserves precision and suits the actual genre; when verification is unavailable, label the proposed change a preference rather than a rule.
triggers: An old guide condemns a word now used by the writer's field or house style.
A diagnosis claims a construction is always ungrammatical based only on one author's preference.
exceptions: An accepted technical term may be clearer for its intended specialists than a looser plain-word substitute.
Do not freeze a historical usage panel's vote as current consensus.
A user's exact quotation or authorized house style is not silently corrected to an editor's taste.

example.before: Request: Proofread the phrase 'data pipeline' in a technical memo. The team's approved glossary uses that term.
example.after: data pipeline
example.why: An established term in the supplied house glossary is not an error merely because it sounds technical.

practice.task: Compare an application and an alternative under the supplied purpose and invariants.
invariants: Preserve the approved term.
Do not invent an error or violate proofreading scope.

alternatives.text: the team's data pipeline
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Only when context needs to distinguish this team's system from another.
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds identification, not a purported grammatical correction.

counterexample.why_not_apply: The supplied definitions establish a real distinction; respect that evidence instead of defending every technical use as a matter of taste.

cards.title: Keep an observation available before turning it into a symbol
cards.mechanism: A supplied detail can carry attention without immediately becoming a metaphor, emotion, or thematic explanation. Compare what the record lets the reader perceive with what an interpretive label adds.
steps: Separate supplied objects, actions and sensory observations from inferred emotional or symbolic meanings.
Try a direct version using only the available detail, then compare any interpretive version against its evidence and the requested genre.
Keep an earned interpretation when it performs needed work; do not manufacture experience or suppress an explicit user's interpretation.
triggers: A scene uses stock mood labels while its supplied objects already distinguish it.
A revision assigns an invented symbolic meaning or psychological state to an observed detail.
exceptions: Interpretation is not forbidden; criticism, analysis and explicitly authorized fiction may require it.
A model has no lived observation of the scene; use the user's record or ask for missing material, never simulate personal witnessing.
The author's noticing exercise is optional; do not require discarding notes or memories.

example.before: Inventory: a folded timetable under an empty chair. Draft: The room was filled with the crushing weight of abandonment.
example.after: A folded timetable lay under the empty chair.
example.why: The sentence makes the supplied particulars available without inventing an emotion, event or symbol.

practice.task: Compare two defensible responses while preserving the stated record and authorized mode.
invariants: Retain the folded timetable, its location, and the empty chair.
Add no cause, sensation or emotional conclusion.

alternatives.text: Under the empty chair lay a folded timetable.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the chair is already the paragraph's topic.
alternatives.tradeoff: Foregrounds location instead of the newly introduced object.

counterexample.text: She wrote in her diary that the empty chair felt like abandonment.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The interpretation is attributed and supplied. Removing it would erase the writer's reported experience.

cards.title: Use the supported name, not an invented technical upgrade
cards.mechanism: Precise names can replace fuzzy category language, but specificity is valuable only when the identification is supported. Historical word origins do not determine current usage.
steps: Identify whether a generic noun obscures a distinction material to the reader.
Use the supplied exact name when known; otherwise retain a category or ask the smallest identification question.
Check uncertain terminology in an appropriate current reference when available; distinguish current sense, social register and etymology.
triggers: A writer calls a specifically identified object a thing, device or substance.
An editor proposes technical diction or an etymological correction without evidence.
exceptions: Do not guess an object's species, model or technical identity to sound exact.
Plain category names can be sufficient for the audience and purpose.
Etymology is background, not a rule overriding established current meaning; dictionary lookup frequency is not a mandatory writing ritual.

example.before: Record: the part is a retaining ring. Draft: The technician removed the small round thing that held the assembly together.
example.after: The technician removed the retaining ring.
example.why: The record supports the exact name; the alternate preserves the function without forcing jargon.

practice.task: Compare two defensible responses while preserving the stated record and authorized mode.
invariants: The technician removed the part.
Do not invent dimensions, materials or tool use.

alternatives.text: The technician removed the ring that held the assembly together.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When the reader needs the function but not the technical label.
alternatives.tradeoff: Less terminologically exact but accessible to a general reader.

counterexample.text: The technician removed an unidentified ring-shaped part.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The record does not establish that it is a retaining ring. A more technical name would add an unsupported fact.

cards.title: Compare sentence behavior instead of scoring a sentence by instinct alone
cards.mechanism: Temporary sentence-per-line layout and plain read-aloud comparison expose repetition, attachment and emphasis that familiar silent reading can hide. A felt snag is an invitation to investigate, not proof of an error.
steps: Compare the original with a temporary sentence-per-line view or a plainly spoken reading, without imposing that layout on the deliverable.
Locate the exact repeated construction, delayed relation or emphasis that changes the reader's experience.
Try a bounded alternative and compare fidelity and function; preserve deliberate repetition or an equally effective original.
triggers: Several sentences have a mechanically repeated opening or an obscured final emphasis.
The writer reports a line sounding awkward but cannot identify the mechanism.
exceptions: Repetition may enact insistence, ritual, parallel facts or comic timing; do not enforce a variety quota.
A model may inspect syntax and likely phrasing but must not claim it heard audio unless audio was actually supplied and inspected.
Sentence-per-line is a diagnostic view, not a required final format; a snag is not by itself an error.

example.before: We checked the seal. We checked the latch. We checked the hinge. Nothing explained the leak.
example.after: We checked the seal, the latch, the hinge. Nothing explained the leak.
example.why: The alternatives compress a routine inventory while retaining the unresolved result; the original remains defensible if its repeated checking is the point.

practice.task: Compare two defensible responses while preserving the stated record and authorized mode.
invariants: All three parts were checked.
No explanation for the leak was found.

alternatives.text: Seal, latch, hinge: we checked all three. Nothing explained the leak.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a brisk inventory fits the speaker's established cadence.
alternatives.tradeoff: The fragment-like opening draws more attention to the list.

counterexample.text: Again we counted. Again we waited. Again we heard nothing.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The repeated opening carries recurrence and frustration; replacing it merely to create variety can weaken the passage.

cards.title: Adjust the relationship to the reader without inventing shared knowledge
cards.mechanism: A temporary version addressed to a particular listener can reveal stiff diction and unearned distance. The useful change is relational clarity, not an automatic informal voice.
steps: Identify the actual audience's knowledge and the speaker's legitimate relation to that audience.
For exploratory editing, compare a direct version addressed to a concrete reader while preserving facts, obligations and distance.
Carry back only improvements appropriate to the final genre; preserve necessary explanation and qualifications.
triggers: A familiar update sounds impersonal, ceremonial or unlike anything the speaker could say.
A generic tone request hides uncertainty about who is speaking to whom.
exceptions: Do not assume shared memories, intimacy or technical knowledge merely because the exercise imagines a friend.
Formal, legal or institutional distance can perform a legitimate function.
Plainness does not prove sincerity or factual truth; do not infer the writer's psychology from wording.

example.before: The occurrence of a delay in my response was attributable to the necessity of checking the figures.
example.after: I replied late because I needed to check the figures.
example.why: Both versions clarify the reported cause without adding an apology, excuse or relationship.

practice.task: Compare two defensible responses while preserving the stated record and authorized mode.
invariants: The reply was late.
Checking the figures caused the delay.

alternatives.text: My reply was delayed while I checked the figures.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When a more reserved professional stance is wanted.
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more distance and less foregrounded personal agency.

counterexample.text: Please retain this exact clause in the signed notice: 'The response period is extended until Friday.'

cards.title: Let a sentence expose a better approach without abandoning the brief
cards.mechanism: Revision can generate new structure and clarify what the writer is trying to say; it is not merely correction at the end. Compare alternative approaches without treating the original plan as sacred or the user's constraints as disposable.
steps: Identify a sentence or relation whose wording reveals an unresolved thought or a more useful organizing question.
When substantive exploration is authorized, try a genuinely different arrangement using the same supported material.
Compare the arrangements against the task contract and repair adjacent sentences affected by the choice; stop when the requested gain is achieved.
triggers: The draft follows an outline that no longer fits its strongest supported material.
The writer keeps shuffling the same words although the underlying relation remains unclear.
exceptions: Outlines, rough drafts and writing in a document are legitimate aids; no-book-exercise prohibition controls the user.
Proofreading does not authorize a new thesis, structure or paragraph order.
Discovery of a better question is not discovery of a new fact; ask for evidence rather than inventing it.

example.before: Outline: celebrate speed. Record: delivery was faster; three checks were missed. Draft: The new system delivered faster. Three checks were missed. Overall, the change was a triumph.
example.after: The new system delivered faster, but three checks were missed. Its speed needs to be weighed against that loss.
example.why: The facts expose a tension the celebratory outline hid; the alternative reorganizes attention without inventing a verdict.

practice.task: Compare two defensible responses while preserving the stated record and authorized mode.
invariants: Delivery was faster.
Three checks were missed.
No unsupported final evaluation of the system.

alternatives.text: Three checks were missed under the new system, even though it delivered faster.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: When reliability is the user's governing concern.
alternatives.tradeoff: Prioritizes the missed checks without making a final cost-benefit judgment.

cards.title: Choose an opening by the work it enables next
cards.mechanism: An opening need not dazzle or summarize the entire piece. Compare what each candidate lets the next sentence do, including its orientation, question and promise.
steps: Try two supported starting points rather than forcing a conventional hook or general introduction.
For each, identify the specific next move it makes possible and whether the body can fulfill its implied promise.
Choose by the task and reader's needs; revisit the opening if later sentences reveal a better entry.
triggers: An introduction clears its throat or advertises significance without entering the actual material.
A clever first sentence sets up a promise the supplied body cannot answer.
exceptions: A summary lead, heading or direct instruction can be the right opening for the genre.
Do not manufacture suspense by withholding safety-critical or decision-critical information.
The exercise does not authorize changing facts or adding dramatic scene detail.

example.before: Record: the archive closes Friday; two boxes remain uncatalogued. Draft: Archives have always played a vital role in preserving history.
example.after: The archive closes Friday. Two boxes remain uncatalogued.

invariants: Closing is Friday.
Two boxes remain uncatalogued.

alternatives.text: Two boxes remain uncatalogued, and the archive closes Friday.

alternatives.tradeoff: Defers the deadline to the end of the first sentence.

counterexample.text: Emergency notice: 'Leave the building now. Use the east exit.'
counterexample.why_not_apply: Direct instruction performs the job; a delayed or evocative narrative opening would obstruct it.
